Financial performance of Air India 
887. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that during 2002-03 Air India had anticipated 
a profit of Rs.100 crores, whereas during April-December 2002, its 
operating income was Rs. 3,612 crores while the operating expenditure 
was Rs. 3,740 crores, resulting in a loss of Rs. 127 crores; and 
(b) if so, what is the actual profit or loss of Air India from 1st April 
2002 to 31st March 2003, together with the reasons therefor and what is 
the projection of profit during 2003-04? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) As per provisional results 
compiled for the period April-December 2002 and for the entire financial 
year 2002-2003, Air India is expected to earn a Net Profit of approx. 65 
crores and Rs. 105 crores respectively. Net results are different from 
operating results as they take into account non operating performance 
as well. The factors attributing to Net Profit are: (i) Low finance/Interest 
cost primarily due to reduction in interest rates in the international market; 
(ii) Dividend of Rs.20 crores received from the subsidiary company, i.e. 
HCT, on account of profit on sale of properties; and (iii) Profit of approx. 
Rs.17 crores on sale of three aircraft to Ariana Afghan Airlines through 
the Ministry of External Affairs. 
As per the budget approved by the Board of Air India for the financial 
year 2003-2004, the Company is ex pected to incur a net loss of Rs. 
55.50 crores. The factors attributing to the loss envisaged for the 
financial year 2003-2004 are (i) Cancellation/withdrawal of flights due 
70 

[29 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
to SARS resulting in drop in traffic and pilots non-cooperation during 
April/May, 2003; (ii) Increase in pric es of aviation turbine fuel; and (iii) 
Overall recessionary trend in the International market. 
Specialized Wing for Airport Security 
888. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any steps have been taken for tightening the security 
measures at airports; 
(b) whether a dedicated wing of  CISF will be given specialized 
training for the security of airports; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) Security measures are in place at all 
airports in the country in accordance with the guidelines issued by the 
International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO). Based on threat 
perception, security measures are further strengthened which inter-alia 
include cent percent physical check of registered baggage, increased 
surveillance at the airport, deployment of Sky Marshals, Quick Response 
Teams, secondary ladder point frisking, increased perimeter patrolling, 
restricting entry of visitors in some areas of airport, etc. 
(b) and (c) CISF deployed at airports are already given specialised 
pre-induction training on aviation security. Subsequently, they are given 
on the job training for one month by the State Police before aviation security 
duties are handed over to them. A two-week's training on aviation security 
at CISF National Institute of Security Academy at Hyderabad is also given 
to them. BCAS and IB also conduct training for CISF personnel.

Rent for using AAl's assets 
†894. SHRI BALKAVI BAIRAGI: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the existing policy for providing assets of Airports Authority of 
India (Hangarland etc.) to State Governments for official purposes; 
(b) the manner in which Airports Authority of India determines the 
rental of barracks and hangars and whet her there is any difficulty to 
permit use of these assets free of cost for non-commercial purposes; 
(c) whether any proposal for waiving off rent of condemend barracks 
and hangars of Directorate General of Civil Aviation has been forwarded 
to the Central Government by Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttaranchal, 
Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh Governments; and 
(d) if so, the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) The allotment of space and land at the 
airport to State Government various airlines and other agencies is 
provided on first come first serve basis against the payment of applicable 
licence fee. 
(b) The rentals for the barracks and hangars is determined keeping 
in view the reasonable return on the capital investment made by the 
Airports Authority of India for creat ing such infrastructures. Since the 
Authority has to work on commercial  principles, the facilities are not 
provided at free of cost. 
(c) and (d) A proposal for waiving off the rent/licence fee has been 
received in respect of Bhopal Airport in Madhya Pradesh. The matter 
has been taken up with the State Government for reconciliation on the 
applicability of licence fee.

Financial performance of Indian Airlines 
896. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether financial position of Indian Airlines has become weak; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the estimated loss of the Airlines in the first quarter of 2003-04; 
and 
87 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2003] 
(d) the steps being taken to improve its finances? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRl RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) After earning continuous profit 
for three years from 1997-98 to 1999-2000, Indian Airlines started 
incurring losses from the year 2000-01 onwards primarily due to reasons 
beyond the control of the airline. The main reasons are as under:— 
(i) Two successive hikes in Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) prices during 
the year 2000. 
(ii)  Increase in landing and navigational charges. 
(iii) Increase in security relat ed expenditure due to sky marshalling 
of flights, secondary frisking of passengers and baggage at 
boarding and ladder points etc. 
(iv)  Increase in aircraft maintenance expenditure. 
(v) Increase in insurance premiums after the terrorists attack at 
Colombo Airport in July, 2001 and following the September 11, 
2001 incidents in USA. 
(c) The Company has incurred an estimated loss of Rs. 44.65 crores 
in the first quarter (April-June) of 2003-04. 
(d) Indian Airlines has taken various measures and working out 
strategies, from time to time and on an on-going basis, to improve its 
financial performance. The steps taken in this regard mainly include the 
following:— 
(i) Comprehensive budgetary cont rol system: whereby actual 
performance is compared with budget estimates, shortfall analysis 
and corrective actions, wherever called for, is initiated on an on-
going basis. 
(ii) Cost-benefit analysis: before undertaking any major project/ 
investment. 
(iii) Cost Control and Economy measures: Control on overtime, 
engagement of casual labour, Staff on Duty (SOD) travel, hotel, 
transport & other crew lay over expenditure, aircraft maintenance, 
freeze on recruitment unless absolutely necessary for operational 
88 

[29 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
reasons, fuel monitoring and tankering, review of uneconomic 
flights, inventory management, outsourcing of services wherever 
feasible/economical.

904. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many fake credit card rackets have been 
busted during the last two years; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken to provide f oolproof system in credit card 
dealings? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) and (b) Reserve Bank of 
India (RBI) have reported that out of 17 card issuing Public Sector Banks, 
State Bank of India and Vijaya Bank have reported incidence of cheating 
on account of use of counterfeit credit cards. In the case of Vijaya Bank, 
and international card was skimmed and used fraudulently at Malaysia 
by the culprits. The amount of loss to the bank was Rs. 0.99 lakh. As a 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2003] 
precaution, the bank has advised its card holders visiting South East 
Asian countries to surrender their cards on their return and obtain fresh 
cards with new numbers. SBI Card s & Payment Services Pvt. Ltd.—a

credit cards involving Rs. 4.88 lakh during the period from April 2002 to 
end-June 2003. Out of this, Rs. 0.72 lakh has been recovered and the 
balance amount of Rs. 4.16 lakh has been treated as loss. 
(c) RBI have reported that banks have been advised to set up internal 
control systems to combat frauds like fraud at application stage, misuse 
of lost/stolen cards and cards not received by genuine applicants, 
counterfeit/altered cards, etc. Fraud prevention committees/task forces 
are in existence which take proactive fraud control and enforcement 
measures. Banks are advised to acti vely participate in such fraud

Failure of banks to recover loans 
905. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Wi ll the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that desp ite sweeping powers given by the 
Securitisation Bill to recover bad de bts, banks have fa iled to recover 
them; 
(b) if so, whether Government have made any investigation in this 
regard; and 
(c) the efforts Government propose to make to accelerate the 
process recovery of loans? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) No, Sir. Under the Securitisation 
& Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest 
Act, 2002,27 public sector banks have issued 32043 notices involving an 
amount of Rs. 11447.13 crores as on 31st May, 2003 and have recovered 
an amount of Rs. 435.68 crores from 8676 cases. The Act has created a 
favourable climate for recovery and induced settlement in several cases. It 
is too early to assess the progress at this stage. 
(b) No investigation appears to be necessary. 
94 

[29 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) Government of India and Reserve Bank of India have advised the 
banks and financial institutions to take several steps for recovery of dues 
such as evolving and implementation of recovery policy by banks, filing 
of suits with civil courts, filing cases with Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs), 
compromise settlement through Settlement Advisory Committees, Lok 
Adalats and monitoring and follow up of NPAs at various levels. Credit 
Information Bureau has also been set up to desseminate information on 
borrowers to the banks. Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) scheme 
has been put place to provide a transparent mechanism for restructuring 
of corporate debts of viable entities facing problems due to internal and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI ANANDRAO VITHOBA ADSUL): (a) As reported by Reserve 
Bank of India (RBI), the following criteria/norms are advised for licensing 
new urban co-operative banks (UCBs): 
• Enhanced entry point (capital) nor ms, ranging from Rs. 25 lakhs 
to Rs. 4 crore, depending on the population of the centre; 
• The capital requirements are halved for banks set up with only 
one branch, or by mahilas/SC/ST and in less developed States. 
Reduced membership/capital requirements are also applicable 
for banks set up in least devel oped States/notified backward 
regions/North-eastern States; 
• Emphasis is made on securing stronger corporate governance 
with minimum eligibility criteria prescribed for promoters of new 
UCBs—of not being a defaulter to any bank/financial institution, 
not being convicted of any criminal offence, should not have any 
criminal proceedings against them, not be associated as director 
with any chit fund/NBFC/cooperative/commercial banks, at least 
two promoters with suitable banking experience or with relevant 
professional qualifications, etc. 
• The business and financial projections submitted by the 
promoters, their background and credentials and their capability 
to direct the affairs of the bank; 
• Factors influencing the viability of the proposed bank, statutory 
framework and the strength of the co-operative movement in the 
State.

obtaining a licence from RBI.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE

service tax and Government's commitment to remove exemptions is 
expected to result in an improvement in the tax-GDP ratio. In 2003-04,

AND NATURAL GAS (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) and (b) 
In order to increase oil and gas production in its areas of operation, 
Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited (ONGC) has taken various

(i) to improve the recovery factor from existing major fields by 
implementing Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR)/lmproved Oil

10,000 crore, which would also help in accelerating oil

frontier areas, as also explore in the deeper layers of the producing 
fields. 
(iii)  to develop faster the newly discovered fields and to step up the 
use of new technologies for seismic surveys, work over, 
stimulation operations, drilling of wells, etc. in producing areas. 
(iv) to develop some of its marginal fields through service contracts. 
(v) to accrete new hydrocarbon re serves through acquisition of 
35,286 Ground Line Kilometre/Line Kilometre (GLK/LK) of two 
dimensional (2D) and 34,834 Sq. Km. of 3D seismic data and 
drilling of 561 exploratory wells in onland and offshore basins.

by 2011-12, which may necessitate 81 per cent import; and

policy?

1011. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that engineers, environmentalists, former 
bureaucrats, scientists, academicians etc., have written to Government 
for a white paper on the proposed inter-linking of rivers in the country; 
(b) if so, the details of the memorandum submitted to Government; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the proposed linking of rivers required 
more power than it will generate; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESORUCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Some 
engineers, environments, former bureaucrats, scientists, academicians 
187 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2003] 
etc., have addressed a letter to Hon'ble Prime Minister and impressed 
that the project for the linking of rivers, needs careful reconsideration 
before proceeding ahead in the matter. In the Memorandum enclosed 
with their letter they have also set forth the reasons for such a 
reconsideration. Conclusions as listed in Memorandum are given in the 
attached statement {See below). 
(c) and (d) The linking proposals under Himalayan and Peninsular 
Components of National Perspective Plan envisage generation of about 
34,000 MW of power. Against this, the requirement of power for lifting 
of water into the link canals is about 4,2000 MW only, as per the 
prefeasibility studies carried out by National Water Development Agency. 
Statement 
Conclusion as listed in Memorandum 
We must hope that the Task Force will consider not merely the 
'modalities' of the 'linking of rivers' but also all the questions raised 
above. Any headlong rush in the pursuit of this chimera will be disastrous. 
Specifically, the following suggestions are placed before the Task Force 
and the Ministry: 
* Take people into confidence as to what the Government plans to 
do, publish a White Paper; 
* make the National Commission's Report (1999) as well as the 
various studies and pre-feasibility and feasibility reports of the 
NWDA widely and easily available to the public; 
* hold hearings, invite comments; make the declared commitment 
to the principles of 'people's participation' and 'stakeholder 
consultation' real; 
* hold discussion with knowledgeable people and institutions 
outside the Government (econo mists, engineers, geographers, 
ecologists, sociologists, agricul tural scientists, scholars and 
institutions concerned with wate r, agriculture, irrigation, and 
problems of rain-fed areas or arid zones, management specialists, 
development studies institutions , voluntary agencies and other 
civil society institutions, and so on) and pay serious attention to 
their questions and apprehensions; 
188 

[29 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
* instead of starting from an a priori proposition about the linking 
of rivers, proceed from the water needs of each areas, consider 
all the available options, and choose the best; 
* focus on efficient, harmonious sustainable intra-basin water 
management first before thinking of importing external water, 
reach the stage of basin-planning before considering inter-basin 
transfers; 
* where a river-linking or long-distance water-transfer proposal 
seems prima facie worth considering, get a thorough, professional 
feasibility report prepared in a fully inter-disciplinary manner, 
internalizing not techno-economic but also environmental, human, 
social, equity, 'gender' and other relevant aspects and concerns, 
and put it through a comprehensiv e, inter-disciplinary, rigorous 
and stringent process of detail ed examination, appraisal and 
approval; 
* let such a project or projects emerge from and be an integral 
part of the planning process, rather than be foisted on that process 
and pre-empt attention and resources from necessary and urgent 
activities; and 
* take up "on a war-footing" (in the Prime Minister's words) a 
national project of extensive, community-led rainwater-harvesting 
(wherever feasible) and watershed development, as also of the 
revival and re-activation of tranditional systems of water 
harvesting, conservation and management (tanks, ahars and 
pynes, johads, etc.), in pursuance of the Prime Minister's clarion 
call at the meeting of the NWRC on 1 April 2002.

Problem of flood and drought in the country 
1024. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are awar e about the problem of certain 
areas in the country facing problem of floods while other areas registering 
perpetual drought; 
(b) if so, whether Government hav e taken any steps to solve the 
problem; and 
(c) 1f so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Various measures that are necessary and are being 
taken by the Central & State Gove rnment to address the problem of 
recurring floods include structural measures as well as non-structural 
measures. The structural meas ures of flood management include 
constructing embankments, reservoi rs, channel improvements, anti-
crosion spurs etc. The non-structur al measures include flood plain 
zoning, flood proofing, disaster preparedness, flood forescating and 
warning etc. Similarly the drought mitigation measures being adopted 
by the Central/State Governments are in the form of short-term, medium-
term and long-term. The short-term measures include execution of 
labour-oriented schemes, transportation of water for drinking purposes 
204 

[29 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
from outside regions, monitoring of ground water, and allowing temporary 
mining of ground water, monitoring water level in reservoirs and strict 
control on releases. The medium-term measures include rainwater 
harvesting and watershed management; and water management in 
irrigated agriculture. The long-term measures include planning and 
creation of surface water storage for drought mitigation. In addition, in 
order to effectively tackle the problems of floods & droughts, the Ministry 
of Water Resoures, then known as the Ministry of Irrigation, formulated 
a National Perspective Plan for water resources development in 1980 
which envisages inter linkages among Peninsular Rivers and Himalayan 
Rivers for optimum utilisation of wa ter resources. The Government of 
India has established the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) 
in 1982 as an autonomous society to carryout water balance and other 
studies and prepare feasibility report s. NWDA has identified 30 links 
under the national perspective for preparation of the feastbility reports 
and has completed feasibility reports of 8 links.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, I am glad to have this opportunity of making my observations on 
the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Bill, 2003, which was 
passed in the Lok Sabha and is now for the consideration of this House. So 
far, the issue of fiscal management, specially in terms of deficit, both fiscal and 
revenue, shrinkage of the revenue reso urces and debt burden, all these are 
important issues and there is a need for putting a brake on the way federal 
finances are being managed. I am happy, while introducing the Bill in Lok 
Sabha in 2000, the hon. Minister also  quoted from the observations of Dr. 
Ambedkar while piloting Article 268, now Article 292 of the Constitution, where 
it was pointed out whether there should be a ceiling on the borrowing power of 
the Union Government and of the State Governments. Now, our Constitution 
was adopted on 26 th January 1950, but successive Finance Ministers did not 
consider it necessary to have a Parliament ary legislation to put a curb on their 
borrowing power. Perhaps, at that point of time, and specially, upto 1981-82 
when, for the first time, we entered into the era of revenue deficit, it was 
considered that prudent fiscal management would be enough and no 
parliamentary law to restrict the borro wing power of the Executive would be 
required. If I remember correctly, at the beginning of the Sixth Plan, the 
Revenue deficit in terms of percentage was insignificant, but perhaps Shri G.M. 
Patel was the last Finance Minister who had the privilege of presenting a 
Budget where there was a net surplus on the revenue account - taking both 
tax and non-tax revenues. And even dur ing the Sixth Plan period except for 
the last year, the revenue deficit in te rms of percentage, did not crors beyond 
one per cent. But, thereafter, the situation became really unmanageable and I 
am glad that the hon. Finance Minister and Leader of the House considers it 
necessary to have a parliamentary legislation to tackle the issue, to tackle the 
problem. But I expect it, especially from my dear colleague, Mr. Jaswant Singh 
that he should be bold enough to take a little more bolder step, especially in 
the context of certain positive macro-ec onomic indicators, in terms of the 
overall inflationary pressure, huge foreign exchange reserves, and the country 
having entered into a regime of current account surplus instead of current

account deficit which was a chronic prob lem that every Finance Minister had 
to face. Therefore, though it is a good step, and a step in the right direction, 
but to my mind, it is a bit hesitant and an uncertain step. Perhaps, because the 
Finance Minister is too cautious and he w ants to review the situation, that is 
why, he has taken Clause 12 in the last  and has said that if there is any 
difficulty in the implementation of the Bill, the necessary corrections will be 
made in two years and not beyond that. Before coming to the various 
provisions of the Bill, I would like to have just one small clarification. It may be 
that I did not hear the Finance Minist er correctly when he introduced the Bill 
yesterday. He pointed out that the total liabilities of the Central Government -- 
if I heard him correctly -- was Rs. 18,00,000 crores. Now, when the Bill was 
introduced in the Lok Sabha in 2000 , in the Statement of Objects and 
Reasons, it is pointed out that the total liabilities of the Central Government are 
above Rs. 12,00,000 crores. My query is: Has the situation deteriorated, 
between 2000 and 2003, to such an extent  that the liability has gone up from 
Rs. 12,00,000 crores to Rs. 18,00,000 crores? If I have heard him wrong, then 
this point need not be clarified. But, if  I heard him correctly, then it requires 
some explanation that why there is such a huge discrepancy in this figure. 
Madam, the question arises, how to control the serious distortions 
which have taken place in terms of fiscal deficit, in terms of revenue deficit and 
in terms of slowing down of the re venue realisation. On earlier occasions, 
while participating in the debate, I have pointed out that there had been some 
serious distortions in the Central fin ances. Take the case of balance from 
current revenue. The deterioration is so sharp! In 1996-97, the negative 
balance was 13,324 crores of rupees. Of course, when I am talking of this 
figure, I am talking of the Centre and the States taken toge ther. Within three 
years, the negative contribution of the Centre and the States taken together, 
has deteriorated from Rs. 13,324 crores in 1996-97 to Rs.92,969 crores in 
1999-2000. And the States ' negative contribution this year--I have calculated 
the combined figure-was roughly 32,000 crores of rupees. Therefore, if you 
exclude 32,000 crores of rupees from th ese 92,969 crores of rupees, then the 
Centre's negative contribution this year is more than 60,000 crores of rupees. 
And that deterioration is taking place with in a span of three years! Therefore, it 
was absolutely necessary to take certain corrective steps. But the legislation, 
to my mind, does not have ad equate teeth. That is why I said that it is a rather 
extremely cautious step. Yes, you ar e committing yourselves and accepting 
the revenue deficit which you

The second point-which I have almost like a parrot repeated on the 
floor of this House umpteen number of ti mes-is that there is no substitute to 
the Government's own revenue, and serious exercises will have to be made to 
augment the Government's own revenue. Even up to 1989-90, the tax-GDP

points, from 11.6 per cent to 9.6 per cent. Instead of moving up, it has come 
down. I am not talking of what, to my mind, would be the ideal situation. The 
tax-GDP ratio, the Centre and the St ates taken together should be anywhere 
around 16 to 18 per cent. But even what it was up to 1989-90, that level of the

about it in his introductory observations.  Of course, he will spell it out at the 
time of the presentation and the formula tion of the Budget, and also at the 
time of making three statements--the Mid-term Fiscal Policy Statement, the 
Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement and the Macro- economic Framework 
Statement. Even before the presentation of the Budget, in the first statement 
he may give some indications. But my point is that the revenue expansion 
brooks no delay. This matter should be taken up immediately. If you can't take 
it up immediately, I don't suggest, by  any stretch of imagination, moving 
vertically. But, surely, there is scope for moving horizontally, both in the case 
of direct taxes and, more so, in the case  of indirect taxes. I don't subscribe to 
the view that there is no scope for having any expansion in the realisation of 
the direct taxes by horizontal expansio n. It can be done not by jacking up the 
rate of taxes, but by better compliance, by bringing  more

The third point is this. The Finance Minister has diagnosed very 
correctly that it is a peculiar situation. Fifty per cent of our normal consumption 
expenditure, today, is met by borrowed resources. Borrowed resources have 
their costs and we are substantiall y depending on high cost borrowed 
resources, though borrowings from the small savings are the costliest. The 
Central Government is not drawing any money from the small savings except 
deducting the cost of rea lisation, which is transferred to the States. But the 
economic impact is there, whether it is to be borne by the State Governments 
or the Central Government. Unless we break this vicious circle to meet our 
normal consumption expenditure, we have to borrow and we have to borrow at 
a high cost; and thereafter a substantial part of our revenue will be used to 
meet the debt servicing. This circle must be broken. Dr. Manmohan Singh took 
some initiative and thereafter it has been followed by you also. When you are 
having substantial foreign exchange reserves, at least, you can utilize a 
sizeable amount of it, depending on what exactly the quantum, for your debt 
repayment so that debt servicing gets reduced. I am happy. In your reply to 
my own question today, you have suggeste d that in the last  year the debt-
servicing ratio, so far as external debt is concerned, has come down from 22 
per cent of GDP to 20 per cent of GDP. But, to my mind, there is no point in 
having this huge amount of foreign exchange reserves, which you can't 
properly utilise, unless there is a dem and for imports and there is massive 
industrial activity or agricultural activi ty or activity in the service sectors. 
Otherwise, the imported components like machineries, technologies, capital 
goods, intermediate products, etc., will not be required and, therefore, they will 
not be utilised. So, to what extent, can you do it? I think, this is one area which 
you should consider.

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE AND MINISTER OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN  JAITLEY): Madam, several hon. 
Members have expressed their opinion, all in support of this Bill. Let me 
clarify, at the very outset, that the ob ject of this Bill, as one of the hon. 
Members obliquely indicated, is not to encourage divorces. Broken marriages 
and divorces have several adverse human consequences. They can create 
emotional distress. They can create social  distress. They can affect the social 
fabric of the society. If, today, we se e in the West, parti cularly the developed 
countries, where the rate of divorces and breaking up of marriage is very high, 
there are countries where the depressi on rate is very high. There are 
countries where the suicide rate is ve ry high. And, one of the reasons for 
demographic change is because a number  of marriages are breaking up. The 
countries where this is happening, wh ere the number of working hands and 
knowledge minds available, really to discharge the functions within their 
growing economies, is not adequate in itself.    So, this is a larger social and 
economic impact which has been 
272 

[29 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA  
created. So, the object, certainly, is not  to encourage divorces. But the object 
of this Bill, as also several other legislations that the Government has 
proposed during the last few years, is, really, that whatever inequities have 
existed in the laws relating to marriages and divorces and various personal 
laws, with the participation and consent of the communities and their leaders, 
and opinion-makers of those communities, we must try and see to it that these 
inequities in themselves are removed. And, slowly, but surely, we have been 
moving in that direction. An hon. Me mber mentioned that we must now have 
procedures under the Christian Law to be  simplified. I must refresh the hon. 
Member's memory that during the last fifty years, at least, three attempts were 
made earlier to correct what were considered by many as some aberrations in 
the Christian law. The man and woman in  their rights were considered to be 
different. The procedures are very cumbersome, because Christianity, as a 
religion, abhor the idea of divorce. Th ey felt marriages are an institution that 
cannot be ended in itself. There was, from several sections of the community, 
a considerable opposition. But, two years ago, when we did make certain 
proposals, with regard to amendments to the Christian Laws, there was, 
initially, a discussion amongst the mem bers of the community and, finally, the 
leaders of the community insisted and,  two years ago, the Indian Divorce Act 
was amended and several provisions of the Indian Divorce Act, which created 
inequities in themselves, were remov ed from the provisi ons of the Indian 
Divorce Act. So, that amendment has already taken place. Madam, people, 
have now, no longer need to go to the High Court for confirmation of divorces. 
Now, the grounds of divorce availabl e to a man and a woman are identical. 
Various parities have been restored and inequities in such have been 
removed. 
Now, I come to maintenance laws. We have amended Section 125 of 
the Cr.P.C. We have removed upper cap of Rs. 500. We have amended 
various other personal laws, including the Special Marriage Act, the Hindu 
Marriage Act, the Christian Marriage Act where we have made provisions for 
payment of maintenance far simpler. No w, these are the various provisions 
which we have amended in various laws over the last few years and this 
amendment is also pursuant to the direction which we have been, slowly, 
following. Now, the reasons which have necessitated these two amendments 
are: The first one is in relation to the jurisdiction of a court where a petition can 
be filed in relation to any of the matrim onial causes of action. I would beg to 
humbly disagree with the hon. Member when he 
273 

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2003]  
said that some provisions of jurisd iction could be removed. One of the 
provisions was, where the marriage had been solemnised, is the court of 
appropriate jurisdiction; where the parti es last resided, is the court of 
appropriate jurisdiction; where the respondent, against whom the action is 
maintained, is the court of appropriate jurisdiction. These were all considered 
appropriate courts, and are still consider ed appropriate courts because if a 
case is contested, then, it  is not the interest of the man and the woman which 
alone is the cause of justice; the obje ct of the judge would be to find out who 
has committed the matrimonial wrong.  Therefore, those would be the 
appropriate courts, within whose jurisdicti on the evidence of that matrimonial 
wrong would be available. So, if the par ty has last resided in Bangalore, and 
the case is transferred, let us say, to  Shimla, then every witness will have to 
travel from Bangalore to Shimla and, t herefore, to say that Bangalore should 
never have the jurisdiction in itself, ma y itself create an inequity. That is not 
one of the objects, as far as the Gove rnment is concerned, behind proposing 
this. The real object is that, with these jurisdictions intact, if a wife presents a 
petition, she should, having gone away from her matrimonial home to some 
other place, or her parents home, or to  some relatives home, be entitled, 
because she is the one who really has been, in a broken marriage, more at the 
receiving end. Most of the Indian wo men even today are not earning. They 
have to depend on relatives or parents, in a broken marriage, for their 
livelihood. Their ability to travel long distances on every date of hearing and 
contest the case is very limited. Theref ore, it is an enablin g provision, which 
gives to the woman in a broken marriage, the right to present a petition in a 
court within whose jurisdiction she is residing after the broken marriage. It is 
an enabling provision, which provides furt her facility to the women. This would 
be of considerable use, as far as women are concerned. 
I am extremely grateful to the hon.  Member, Shrimati Bimba Raikar, 
who had initially suggested it to be brought forward as a Private Member's Bill. 
The Women's Commission had supported this idea. The Law Commission had 
supported this idea. Therefore, this is a proposal, which is really a beneficial 
proposal for women, which has received support all along. 
As far as the second provision, in relation to the enlargement of time 
for filing an appeal, is concerned, this has one more object, besides the 
objects which the hon. Members had pl eaded. In a number of matrimonial  
cases,   thirty  days'  time  is  being  given,  the  woman  being

inadequate in her resources at times, is not able to contest. Cases have also 
come to notice, where ex parte orders are obtained, and once, ex parte orders 
are obtained, by either not serving the woman, or, by giving a wrong address, 
and after the ex parte decree, if within thirty days  no appeal is filed, the man 
marries once again. And once the woman realises that there is a new family 
which has come into existence -- ther e are hundreds and thousands of cases 
all over the country - it is then that she realises that a divorce has been 
procured behind her back. When she goes back to the court, she  told that 
thirty days' period is over, and she is unable to file the appeal. Now, in case 
this divorce is set aside, questions have arisen as to what would happen to the 
second marriage, what would happen to the children born out of the second 
marriage, and this would create further complications. As a result of this, the 
Supreme Court itself, in one of the judgm ents, has suggested that, at least, to 
bring some end to this practice, if not entirely, we should enlarge the period, as 
far as the filing of the appeal is c oncerned. Therefore, for people who are 
victims of ex parte orders, particularly which are obtained behind their back, or, 
people who may have to raise resources in order to file an appeal, because 
appeals in a divorce case would lie to the High Court, from a moffusil court or 
from a district court, somebody would have  to travel to the State Capital to go 
to the High Court, resources would be required, women are inadequate in their 
resources; so, 30 days itself is an inadequate period. This period should be 
extended to 90 days. This was the purpose behind the suggestion. Therefore, I 
am extremely obliged to the hon. Members, who have supported this particular 
suggestion of enhancing this period. Ye s, it is very right, what the Hon. 
Member, Mr. Gowda, pointed out that something has to be done in order to 
improve the efficiency of the courts, where these cases are being heard. The 
Act itself mentions that a divorce case should normally get over in six months 
to one year. That should be the normal period. But because of the workload of 
the courts, and the inadequate infrastr ucture in the courts, all across the 
country, this, at times, takes a lot of time . Now, this time period itself causes a 
lot of distress because if years and year s altogether, and literally decades are 
spent between the original cases and also  the appeals, people, besides being 
harassed emotionally, are gaining in years.... people are gaining in years, 
people are gaining in age. So, the prospec ts of settling in life after the divorce 
also get diluted or diminished. And, theref ore, this adds to the distress. In fact, 
distress becomes destitution in some cases because such may be the adverse 
consequences of delays in these cases.   Therefore, we have been

RAJYA SABHA [29 July, 2003]  
STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Incident of attack by terrorists on Tanda Army Cantonment at Akhnoor In 
Jammu and Kahsmlr, on July 22,2003 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): 
Madam Deputy Chairperson, the statement that I am going to present to the 
House was actually made availabl e to the Secretariat on the 24 th of July. But 
certain circumstances intervened, an d I was not called upon to make the 
statement. 
I would like to inform the House abo ut the unfortunate incident of 
terrorist attack in Tanda Cantonment at Akhnoor In Jammu and Kashmir on 
July 22, 2003.   I have visited the site in the morning of July 23, 2003. 
On July 22, 2003 at about 0550 hours,  three terrorists, one In civilian 
dress and two in combat uniform with khaki caps (one was wearing the 
epaulettes of Pakistan Army Lieutenant and Janbaz insignia) disembarked 
from a civil truck in front of the EME Battalion gate of Tanda Cantonment. The 
sentry at the gate immediately challeng ed them and opened fire. One terrorist 
was killed on the spot, and in the ensuing firefight one sentry was killed and 
one injured. The other terrorists evaded fire of the sentry and rushed inside 
the unit lines lobbing grenades and firing  indiscriminately. In the process, a 
total of two Junior Commissioned Office rs (JCOs) and four Other Ranks (Ors) 
were killed and two JCOs and four Ors were wounded. The Quick Reaction 
Team (QRT) of the unit killed the second terrorist. 
By 0630 hours, the Quick Reaction Team from neighbouring units 
were also moved to the location. A detailed search of the area was carried out 
till 1030 hours. After searching the unit  Unas and the adjoining area under the 
supervision of senior officers of local formation, it was assessed that the area 
had been cleared of the terrorists. 
At about 1300 hours, Lt. Gen. Hari Prasad, GOC-in-C, Northern 
Command, and Lt. Gen. TPS Brar, GOC , 16 Corps along with their staff 
officers visited the site to review the situation. As these officers were moving 
in the area, one terrorist emerged from the bushes in a nala, which passes 
through the unit lines and lobbed two grenades on them. ...    The 
282 

[29 Jury, 2003] RAJYA SABHA  
Terrorist   later  blew  himself   up. However, seven  officers,  including  GOC-in-C,  
hern   Command,  and   the  Corps  Commander  received   minor   injuries   due 
to  the  grenade  blasts,  except  Brig. V.K. Govil,  Deputy  Director,  EME, 16 
Corps,  who  later succumbed   to his injuries at 1630 hours.  
As a result of the terrorist attack, eight army personnel (one Officer, two 
JCOs and five ORs) were killed and thirteen (seven Officers, two JCOs and four 
Other Ranks) were wounded. All the three terrorists were killed, and three AK 
rifles and three pistols were recovered. The driver of the truck in which the 
terrorists came has been taken into custody and is being interrogated. 
A lesser known militant outfit, 'Al Shuhda Brigade J&K', has claimed 
responsibility for the attack stating, "the attack on the camp was carried out to 
protest visiting Pakistani Opposition Leader, Maulana Fazlur Rehman's remarks that 
the Line of Control should be converted into a permanent border and the 
Kashmir Issue should be resolved within the framework of the Shimla Agreement". 
The Identity of the three terrorists has not yet been established. 
I may inform the House that adequate measures have been taken 
to ensure security of vulnerable areas by way of gathering intelligence 
inputs, reinforcing the security mechanisms, intensifying patrolling and 
employing Quick Reaction Teams. In addition to security measures in 
position, special strategies are being devised to effectively combat terrorist 
attacks.      ......  
I would like to further inform the hon. Members that an Investigation 
Into the incident has already been ordered. I would like to assure the House 
that if the Investigation establishes any lapse in the enforcement of security 
measures by the Army, stringent action will be taken against those found 
responsible.

been observed by a whole lot of school children sitting up there. And we 
sometimes wonder why people think about us the way they think. 
That apart, three major terrorist attacks, at Kaluchak, Tanda and 
Srinagar, sometime ago, were on units, which are facing the main road. Have 
we not devised measures for this yet? The terrorist attack, which deserves 
and requires -- I am sure the Defence Ministry is doing it, the Army is doing it -
- far greater investigation than the Tanda attack, is the attack on Sanjuan. And 
while these things are unfortunate, a conflicting situation is there, these things 
will happen. There ha ve been a series of such a ttacks; this is not the first 
attack; it will not be the la st attack either. But I do think that we have to devise 
a method -- no method can be foolproof -- based on the pattern of attacks, 
because fidayeen attacks are now more or less commonplace. Human bombs 
will come; they have not yet come, but they will come. We should plan on that. 
We should urgently devise  the details of attacks based on the pattern of such 
attacks, which are taking place. Three of these attacks are on units, which are 
facing the road. 
I express my condolences for the m en who were killed in this attack 
and the previous attacks. We must not lose heart; these attacks will continue. I 
am sure, we will find a way to stop these attacks. I read in the media that 
operations are being intensified. They have to be intensified. The operations in 
Jammu & Kashmir hold the key to the future of our talks with Pakistan. We 
have to intensify our operations and we  have to ensure that such attacks, 
while they will occur -- attempts will be made and some will be successful -- 
are definitely cut down. I understand that the truck driver has been taken into 
custody. It would be interesting to note where he came from, how these 
people got along. I wish the defence fo rces and the Ministry of Defence the 
best of luck in their efforts.

[29 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA  
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES : First let me thank Shri Shankar Roy 
Chowdhury for his observations and assure him that efforts are being 
made to see as to how one can deal with these fidayeens. to the extent 
possible. It is very rightly observed that fidayeen attack is something which 
can never be found out before it act ually happens. Therefore, the Army 
and the security forces are at a great disadvantage when they have to deal 
with the situation where terrorists come loaded with grenades and other 
explosives with their intention to die. In this process, they also take a few 
other lives. The hon. Member asked a question as to how the second 
attack came about. The first attack was in the early hours of morning. After 
the fire-fighting was over, it became  known that there was another person. 
A search was conducted and units from other centres were also called in 
and joined the search: This camp is located in a place where there is a 
very thick forest, right inside the cantonment campus. The length of the 
forest is about one kilometer on both sides  of the tarred road. It is a thick 
forest with nalas and rocks. We can call it a 'jungle'. That particular terrorist 
was hiding in the bushes in a nala and obviously he had camouflaged 
himself in such a way that nobody could find him out where he was hidden. 
At 1 O'clock, a signal was given that the entire place had been sanitized 
and the senior officers might come. At about 1.30 p.m., the senior officers 
reached there. I have already mentioned their names and designations. 
They went around to see the area where the action had taken place 
earlier. When they reached that particular nala, the third terrorist jumped 
out from the place where he was hiding and threw two grenades one after 
the other. He also blew himself up with grenades that he had tied to his 
own body. Now, one can make a point that greater care should have been 
taken by those who were going around, but if one goes to that terrain and 
has a look at that terrain, one woul d understand that such  a situation, I 
won't say inevitable, but such a situation is possible. That is my reply to the 
query. Thank you, Madam.

Statement 
(a) The State Government of J&K have in formed that a total of 1,11,932 
Yatris have registered for Amarnath Yatra this year. However, the number of 
persons who could have Darshan would depend on various factors like 
weather/climatic conditions, security threat, etc. 
(b) It is the responsibility of the State Government of J&K to provide 
security and make all other arrangements for the Amarnath Yatra. Central Police 
Forces are deployed in J&K as an aid to the State Government, keeping in view 
the overall security scenario and availability of these Forces. Like every year, 
additional forces have been provided to the Government of J&K to make security 
arrangements for the Amarnath Yatra 2003. 
The State Government have info rmed that elaborate security 
arrangements have been made for Amarnath Yatra at the base camp, along the 
track as well as at the Holy Cave. As  regards catering facilities, the State 
Government has issued necessary license s for operating lungars at different 
places along the track. 
(c) The expenditure on the Amarnath Yatra is borne by the State 
Government of J&K. However, Government of India is only assisting the 
State Government of J&K through deployment of additional Security Forces. 
The State Government has constituted an Amarnath Yatra Shrine Board for the 
smooth conduct of the Yatra. 
(d) The number of Yatris registered this year is slightly higher than the 
actual visited during Amarnath Yatra 2002, which was 1,10,793.

Power Position in Gujarat 
*151. DR. A.K. PATEL: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that power shortage continues in Gujarat despite 
taking steps in this regard; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the total requirement, availability and shortage of power as on June 
30, 2003 in Gujarat; and 
(d) the steps proposed to be taken to meet the shortage of power in 
Gujarat? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
Yes, Sir. Power shortage continues in Gujarat. Average energy shortage 
during April-June, 2003, as ascertained from Gujarat Electricity Board was of 
the order of 12.7% and peaking shortage 18.7%. 
30 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) The shortage is mainly on account of growth in demand outstripping 
the growth in generation and generation capacity addition. 
(c) According to Gujarat Electricity Board, the total availability as on 
30th June, 2003 was 6060 MW as against a demand of 6290 MW 
representing a shortage of 230 MW. 
(d) Supply and distribution of electricity is the responsibility of the State 
Government. Electricity, being a concurrent subject, Government of India 
supplements the efforts of State Government by setting up power plants in 
Central Sector through Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs. Gujarat 
has a firm allocation of 1538 MW in Central Generating Stations (CGS) in 
Western Region (WR. In addition, the following steps have been/being taken in 
order to mitigate power shortage in Gujarat:—  
(i) Gujarat has been allocated 164 MW from unallocated quota of CGS 
in WR and 80 MW from unallocated quota of NTPC stations in Eastern 
Region (ER. 
(ii) Besides capacity addition of 431  MW in State Sector and 500 MW 
in Private Sector in Gujarat, generation capacity of 5367 MW in 
Central Sector in Western Region and 1450 MW multi-state project 
(Sardar Sarovar Hydro Project) is planned to be set up during 10th 
Plan in which Gujarat will have entitlements. 
(iii) Implementation of Renovation, Modernization and Life Extension 
(R&M & LE) Schemes for old and inefficient generating units for 
overall improvement in generation performance. 
(iv) Demand Side Management, promotion of energy efficiency and 
energy conservation measures. 
(v) Enhancement in evacuation of surplus power from Eastern Region to 
other regions by setting up of inter-regional links. With the 
commissioning of 400 KV Rourkela-Raipur double circuit 
transmission line, the two regional grids viz. Eastern and Western 
Grids have been connected in synchronous mode. Gujarat is also a 
beneficiary of ER power. 
31 

RAJYA  SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
(vi) Government of India has approved the Accelerated Power 
Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) which is intended 
for up-gradation of sub-transmission and distribution in densely 
electrified zones in the urban a nd industrial areas and improvement 
in commercial viability of State Electricity Boards by reducing the 
aggregate technical and commercial (AT&C) losses. During the year 
2002-03, the Government of India has sanctioned sub-transmission 
and distribution (ST&D) projects amounting to Rs. 1035.80 crores 
for up gradation of sub-transmission and distribution in the State of 
Gujarat.

Gold Wealth Beneath Deccan Plateau 
*155.  MISS MABEL REBELLO: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that vast untapped gold wealth lies beneath 
Deccan plateau and it is proposed to exploit these dormant untapped 
potentials; 
(b) the progress made in mining of Huti region gold mines in Karnataka 
and other similarly placed mines in the country; and 
(c) the reasons for lagging behind Australia in gold mining when both 
the countries have similar geographical characteristics such as rock formation 
and the soil beneath surface? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF MINES (SHRI 
RAMESH BAIS): (a) As per Geological Survey of India (GSI), a subordinate 
office under the Ministry of Mines, the geological set up below the Deccan 
Plateau does not suggest occurrence of vast untapped gold wealth. 
(b) In Hutti region, Karnataka, Hutti Gold Mines Limited (HGML), a 
Government of Karnataka Undertaking, operates two units i.e. (i) The 
Hutti Gold Unit (HGU) - comprising Hutti Gold Mines (under ground), 
Uti (Open-cast Mines) and Hirab-Buddini (Exploratory mine), in Raichur 
District and (ii) Chitradurga Gold Unit (CGU) - comprising Ajjanahalli 
(open-cast mine) in Tumkur District and G.R. Halli (exploratory 
underground mine) in Chitradurga District. During the year 2002-2003, 
HGML produced 2709 kgs. of Gold. 
The other gold mines of Bharat Gold Mines Limited (BGML) in the 
Kolar Gold Fields of Karnataka and in Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh have 
been closed due to uneconomic operations. 
(c) Even though there is similarity in the geological setup, structure, 
tectonics and metaliogeny between Yilgarn and Pilbara cartons of 
Australia and Dharwar Craton of Peninsular India, the extent of 
mineralization can vary from craton to  craton. In India the mining has 
been limited to a few relatively high tenor deposits of a minimum 3 g/ 
tonne of primary gold. The occurrences are few and wide apart. In 
40 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Australia the number of reported gold occurrences is much more and both 
underground and opencast mechanized mining is practiced. 
Studies on Abnormal Increase in Summer Temperature 
*156. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the disaster management wing of Home Ministry is aware 
of the fact that several parts of the country, mainly Andhra Pradesh, 
recorded unprecedented high temperature in the summer of 2003; 
(b) whether any agency studies the reas ons for the abnormal increase in 
the average summer temperature in the States like Andhra Pradesh; 
(c) if so, the findings thereof; 
(d) if not, whether Government intend to ask any of our scientific 
agencies to find the scientific reasons for the unusual phenomenon; and 
(e) the action plan to save the poor people from calamity of heat wave 
during summer? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SWAMI CHINMAYANAND): (a) During 2003, heat wave conditions in 
Andhra Pradesh prevailed for a duration of 27 days from 16th May to 11th 
June, whereas in normal cases, it lasts only for about a week or so. Regions 
extending from Rajasthan to coastal Orissa and Andhra Pradesh across 
Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra are prone to heat waves. Its occurrence year 
after year varies in space and time from one region to another. 
(b) and (c) According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD), this 
year a cyclonic storm development over the Bay of Bengal and remained over 
the sea for about 10 days (10-19 May. It had a prolonged influence on the flow 
pattern over the country even after its dissipation. This caused the dry and hot 
northwesterly winds to blow over the peninsula leading to heat wave 
conditions over Andhra Pradesh and its prevalence for an unusualy longer 
duration. Pre-Monsoon showers during summer generally bring respite from 
rising maximum temperatures and consequent improvement in heat wave 
conditions. But this year the 
41 

RAJYA  SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
absence of such rainfall activity significantly contributed to the severity of 
heat wave conditions in Andhra Pradesh. The delay in the onset of the 
monsoon this year also favoured the continuance of heat wave conditions for 
a longer period in June. 
The impact of the heat wave conditions  was also felt rather acutely this 
year due to the prevalence of drought conditions in some regions because of 
poor monsoon rains last year. 
(d) The State Governments concerned take necessary steps to mitigate 
the impact of this problem.

Protection to Indian Garment Exporters in WTO 
1170. SHRI G.K. VASAN: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government propose to take steps to protect the interest of 
Indian garments exporters in WTO; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
BASANAGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Government have been 
taking appropriate steps to protect the interests of Indian textiles export industry 
including garments in the WTO. Some of the recent steps taken are given 
below:- 
170 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(i) India has raised a dispute under the Dispute Settlement Mechanism of 
WTO challenging the zero cutoms duty concession accorded by European 
Communities to the ready-made garments and made-up articles originating 
from some of our competing countries under the special tariff arrangements to 
combat drug production and trafficking of its new GSP Scheme, which are 
perceived by India to cause adverse trade effects on our industry. 
(ii) The United States had on 31st January 2003 requested WTO's 
Committee on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures that the export 
competitiveness of textile and apparel exports from India be determined on the 
basis of a computation undertaken by  the WTO Secretariat in accordance 
with Article 27.6(b) of the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing 
Measures. The products for which the request was made included all tex tiles 
and apparel products under Harmonized System Nomenclature chapters 50-
59 and 60-63. India has sought certain clarifications from the WTO 
Secretariat in this regard. 
(iii) India along with the certain members of International Textiles & 
Clothing Bureau (ITCB) made a submission in the WTO General Council for

Cauvery and Krishna rivers and action taken by Government with regard

SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I beg to call the attention 
of the Minister of Water Resources to the situation arising out of disputes over 
the sharing of inter-state river waters of Cauvery and Krishna rivers and 
action taken by Government with regard thereto. 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI) : Sir, the dispute relating to sharing of Cauvery water among States of 
Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Pondicherry was referred to the Cauvery 
Water Disputes Tribunal (CWDT) constituted on June 2, 1990. The Tribunal has 
not submitted its final report and decision. 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
The CWDT had in June, 1991, passed an interim order directing the 
State of Karnataka for releasing water fr om its reservoirs so as to ensure 205 
thousand million cubic ft. (TMC) of water in Mettur reservoir of Tamil Nadu in 
a water year, in fixed monthly and weekly pattern. The Tribunal had also given 
certain clarifications in April, 1992 and December, 1995, on its Order of June, 
1991. 
The Central Government had published the Order of the Tribunal 
under section 6 of the Inter State Wa ter Disputes (ISWD) Act, 1956 in 1991, 
thus, making the Order final and binding on the parties to the dispute. The 
Order of the Tribunal is to be given effect to by the party States. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI NILOTPAL BASU) in the Chair] 
Further, under the provisions of section 6 A of the ISWD Act, 1956, 
the Central Government has notif ied a Scheme called Cauvery Water 
(implementation of the Or der of 1991 and all subsequent Related Orders of 
the Tribunal) Scheme, 1998, consisting  of Cauvery River Authority and 
Monitoring Committee. The Cauvery Rive r Authority consists of the Prime 
Minister as Chairperson and Chief Minist ers of the basin States as members. 
The authority has held six meetings so far, and the Monitoring Committee has 
held 17 meetings. 
Sir, regarding Krishna Water Dispu tes, the Central Government 
constituted the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (KWDT) in April, 1969, for 
adjudication of the water disputes of  Krishna. The Krishna Water Disputes 
Tribunal submitted its report and decision in 1976. The decision was published 
by Central Government in the Official Gazette on 31.5.1976. As per the KWDT 
direction, at any time after 31 st May, 2000, the order of the KWDT may be 
reviewed or revised by a competent authority or Tribunal. 
The Central Government received requests under Section 3 of the 
Inter-State River Water Disputes (ISRWD) Act, 1956, from the States of 
Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pr adesh in October, 2002, December, 
2002 and January, 2003 respectively requesting for constitution of a Krishna 
Water Disputes Tribunal under section 4 of the ISRWD Act, 1956, and 
referring to the tribunal for adjudication and decision, the water disputes and 
matters connected therewith or relevant to water disputes emerging from the 
letters of complaint.   The constitution of a second Tribunal for Krishna

SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nomin ated): Madam, the essence of 
the Cauvery dispute is a c onflict of interests between Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, 
Kerala, and Pondicherry. Any fair sharing would have to provide for the 
legitimate interests of all the four parties. The time has come to rise above 
narrow political considerations and arrive at a settlement that ensures justice to 
all the aggrieved parties. Rainfall dist ribution over short periods in the 
catchment area of a river is a fact or that comes up when assessing the 
quantity of river-water needed for surface irrigation. Over short periods, the 
rainfall situation in catchment areas and in the basin of the river will vary from 
year to year. Thus, arrangements of water distribution and/or sharing made on 
the basis of averages wi ll not often work in real time. Near continuous 
monitoring of rainfall in all years, t herefore, becomes esse ntial. This means 
that technical experts as well as representatives of farmers'

included in CRA. Is the Government considering expansion of the Cauvery 
Regulatory Authority (CRA)? During floods, Tamil Nadu will be used as a 
drainage area by Karnataka. Such flood water overflows cannot be used in a 
planned manner. Thus, any arbitrating authority on the sharing of Cauvery 
waters should not only indicate the quantum of water to be supplied by 
Karnataka to Tamil Nadu, but also specify the period and intervals over which 
such deliveries are to be effected. Unfo rtunately, the Governments of the two 
principal contending States  have, over the years,  generated and fostered 
strong sentiments among the general public, which tend to limit their own 
negotiating freedom and flexibility. The Cauvery is a fabled river with strong 
historical, religious and cultural asso ciations in both Karnataka and Tamil 
Nadu. In both States, all parties tend to take a strong stand on this issue, 
making it risky for whichever party is in power to give the impression of being 
weak or failing to project the interests of the State. That is why this dispute has 
become so intractable. According to late  Shri S. Guhan, an administrator and 
academician who authored the Cauvery River Dispute which represented an 
authoritative and scholarly track on the Cauvery issue, and I quote, "A 
settlement of the Cauvery di spute, if it is to be settled in the long term, will 
require two conditions to be met. First, it must be fair and equitable to all the 
basin States and perceived as such by them. Secondly, it is necessary 
politically to create a spirit of goodwill and cooperation during the process of 
arriving at a settlement, and to sustain it thereafter when the agreement begins 
to be implemented. What effort has the Central Government made to create 
this climate of goodwill between the contentious parties? Given the uncertainty 
of water release, the cultivation of the Kuruvai crop in Tamil Nadu will be risky 
in most years. Farmers here must be weaned away from the concept of the 
Kuruvai crop as a non-negotiable one. Perhaps, the time has come to demand 
a national crop pattern policy. So, in drought-hit Marathwada, farmers are 
dissuaded from growing sugarcane, and, in the water-scarce Cauvery delta, 
farmers are dissuaded from producing paddy, both water-guzzling crops. Has 
the Government considered putting into place this National Crop Pattern 
Policy? From the point of view of assured water availability, the cropping 
season of rice in the deltaic areas of  Tamil Nadu can only be for eight months 
from August to March. Even this period cannot continuously be used for rice 
because of intervening cloudy and wet weather months from mid October to 
mid December. So,' we can have a rice crop from the beginning of September

just a local issue. Rivers are a part of the country's natural resources and they

to this conclusion not on the merits of the case, but because it had no 
jurisdiction on the matter. Consequently, referring this issue to a new Tribunal

of the Andhra State Act, 1953. What is the Government doing in this regard?

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
With your permission, I would like to say a few words about the 
Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2003. 
India is an active and prominent member of the International 
Maritime Organisation (IMO), the spec ialised U.N. body responsible for 
establishing and enforcing world standards  in maritime shipping. We enjoy a 
high reputation as a leading maritime country and as a major supplier of 
officers to the world maritime industry. 
Apart from the image that India carries as a world class maritime 
country strictly adhering to international norms end regulations, it also has 
international obligation to continuously upgrade the quality of its shipping. 
Laws pertaining to shipping and maritime affairs have global relevance. Our 
ships have to trade internationally and could be subjected to inspections at 
foreign ports to check their compliance with IMO Conventions and protocols 
whose status keeps changing. Similarly, foreign flagships will also be 
subjected to inspections when they visit Indian ports with a view to protecting 
our waters from environmental hazards. In order to implement the conventions 
and protocols to which India has become a party and to be in line with 
international standards, India is required to incorporate the provisions of these 
conventions and protocols in our merchant shipping legislation. We have to be 
dynamic and responsive to both need and time, and the present effort is to 
incorporate the provisions of the c onventions and protocols acceded to by 
India in the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. Once the proposed amendments 
are approved by Parliament, India will be able to keep up with its international 
obligations. 
The International Maritime Organisation adopted in 1973 the 
International Convention for Prevention  of Pollution from Ships, 1973 
(MARPOL 1973), which was amended by adoption of Protocol in 1978. The 
MARPOL 1973 and Protocol of 1978 thereto, together known as MARPOL 
73/78 seeks to achieve complete elimination of pollution of the marine 
environment by oil and other harmful substances and minimization of 
accidental discharge of such substances by prescribing a package of 
requirements of design, construction, survey and other certification norms with 
respect to discharge of sewage and garbage into the sea. 
MARPOL 73/78 has six Annexes specifying the technical 
requirements to be complied by ships for the purpose of safety of life at sea 
260 

[30 July, 20031 RAJYA SABHA 
as well as prevention of pollution from ships. In accordance with Article 14 of 
the MARPOL 1973 and Article II of its 1978 Protocol, the provisions of 
Annexes I and II are mandatory for contra cting States while implementation of 
Annexes III, IV and V was optional. In dia acceded to MARPOL 1973, as 
modified by its Protocol of 1978 alo ng with Annexes I and II, by depositing the 
Instrument of Accession with IMO on 24th September, 1986. The instrument of 
accession deposited by India contained a declaration "that the Government of 
the Republic of India shall not be bound by the provisions of Annexes III, IV 
and V of the said Convention." It was decided not to accede to these annexes 
because by that time, major maritime States had not acceded to these three 
optional annexes: It was decided to firs t understand the imp lications of the 
provisions contained in these annexes. As a number of countries have since 
acceded to these annexes, India has also acceded to these three annexes to 
ensure that Indian ships are not targeted for non-compliance while visiting the 
ports of such countries. Also, accession to these annexes would enable Indian 
to take steps as per the convention to prevent pollution in India waters. 
-Article 15(2) of the Convention, as amended by the Protocol of 1978, 
stipulates that the optiona l annexes shall enter into force internationally, 
twelve months after the date on which not less than 15 States, the combined 
merchant fleets of which constitute not less than fifty per cent of gross 
tonnage of world's merchant ships, have become parties to it. As on 30 th 
November, 2002, the Annexes III, IV and V have been ratified or acceded to 
by 105, 89 and 110 States respec tively. The percentages of combined 
merchant fleet belonging to these Stat es who have become parties to these 
optional Annexes are 82.95, 51.14 and 89.26, respectively. Annexure III and 
Annexure V have come into force inte rnationally on 1.7.1992 and 31.12.1988 
respectively. Annexure IV will come into force on 27.9.2003. 
The main advantage arising from ratifying these Annexes is that the 
Indian as well as foreign vessels plying on overseas trade world-wide would 
automatically follow the universal st andards on the subject. Once these 
Annexes are acceded to, the reception facilities as contained in these 
Annexes are to be provided by the Ports where vessels call. This will, in turn, 
help us to develop service facilities in Indian Ports comparable to standards 
available elsewhere. 
261 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
[THE VICE CHAIRMAN (SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY) in the Chair] 
The system of prevention of pollu tion (i) by harmful substances 
carried by sea in packed forms and (ii) by sewage from ships, as well as the 
Waste and Garbage Management for disposal of garbage from ships in Port, 
etc. could be made mandatory so as  to ensure cleaner waters. Further, 
ratification of the Annexes under c onsideration may ensure avoiding any 
unreasonable application of strict Port State Control on Indian ships elsewhere 
in the world, thereby boosting the Indian maritime services. 
The Government of India has now decided to accede to the optional 
Annexures as the MARPOL 1973 and its Protocol of 1978 strengthened such 
anti pollution measures by introduci ng adequate design and constructional 
aspects of ships so as to control pollut ion of the sea by oil escaping into the 
sea, following marine casualties of t ankers. Besides, these two instruments 
are also intended to control pollution of the sea from: 
(a) harmful    substances    carried    in    package    forms,    freight 
containers, portable tankers and road or rail tank wagons; 
(b) noxious liquid substances in bulk; 
(c) sewage from ships; and 
(d) garbage from ships. 
To implement the provisions of the said Convention and the Protocol, 
the present Bill contains  amendments to 12 sections from section 356A to 
3560 under part XI A of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. 
Annexes I to V to MARPOL 73/78 contain many technical details and 
operational matters which often change with progress made in the sphere of 
technology, safety and environmental st andards. Therefore, it is not desirable 
to put such details in the body of t he Merchant Shipping Act since that would 
involve changing the Act frequently with th e changes in the provisions of the 
Annexes I to V of MARPOL 73/78. As su ch, it is proposed to amend sections 
356 E and 356 O to confer powers on the Central Government to make rules 
to prescribe these technical and operat ional requirements prescribed by the 
MARPOL 73/78 and its Annexes as amended from time to time.

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
With the proposed amendments, India will not only be able to meet 
its international commitments arising out of accession to Annexures III, IV and 
V to MARPOL 73/78 but also will be at par with the systems and requirements 
of other advanced maritime nations.
