SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhra Prades h): Sir, I rise to support the 
Bill brought by the hon. Minister for Sh ipping for the consideration of this 
august House. The aims and objectives of this Bill are laudable. Though the 
Bill before us is a small one, it aims at maintaining the ecological balance and 
preventing ships, oil tankers, voyage ships, etc., from polluting our waters. 
Clause 356B(e) deals with the Convention which covers accidental and 
operational oil pollution as well as pollution by chemicals, goods in packed 
form, sewage, garbage and air pollution.   But, I would like 
266 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
to know from the hon. Minister, when we are a party to the International 
Convention for Prevention of Pollution from Ships adopted by the International 
Maritime Organisation in 1973, which was amended by adoption of Protocol in 
1978, what are the compelling reasons that the Government of India have 
been facing over these 25 years for bringing this legislation before the 
Parliament. On the one hand, you are saying that we are an active member of 
the IMO and, on the other, t here is an enormous delay in implementing the 
Resolutions of IMO and that too when th ose Resolutions are beneficial to our 
country. At the same time, sub-clause (h) of the same clause deals with 
noxious, that is, poisonous liquid subs tances. But, what about the poisonous 
gases that emanate from various oil tankers or ships? Why have you 
exempted the poisonous gases from the purview of clause 356B? 
Sir, I welcome the inclusion of clauses 356C and 356D which deal 
with the issue of pollution prevention ce rtificate. Under these clauses, you are 
making it mandatory for the Indian oil tankers or other ships to obtain pollution 
prevention certificate to proceed to sea. I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister whether it is true that the Maritime Environment Protection Committee 
of the IMO, of which we are an active member, in its 49 th Session held in 
London on 14th July, 2003, resolved to amend the Oil Tanker Regulations in the 
MARPOL Convention. If that is true, I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister the details of the meeting and how it affects our shipping industry. 
The European Union Transport Council has unanimously agreed on the EU's 
proposal and banned the aged single-hu ll tankers from entering into the 
European waters. This grossly affects the SCI's fleet, since more than 40% of 
its fleet constitute single-hull ships. The EU has already banned the vessels 
aged more than 23 years and built before 1982. So, under these 
circumstances, how is the Ministry goi ng to tackle the challenges that are 
going to be faced by the Indian shipping industry? 
The next point, which I would like to make, is about the tax system in 
the shipping industry. The industry has been persistently requesting the 
Government of India for introduction of tonnage tax in place of the existing 
corporate tax. The corporate tax is standing as an impediment in the growth of 
our shipping industry and making it difficult to compete with international 
freight. In January, 2002, the Rakesh Mohan Committee recommended the 
immediate introduction of tonnage tax syst em on the profits of the shipping 
industry.   But for the reasons best known to the hon. 
267 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July. 2003] 
Minister, it has not yet been im plemented. Then tonnage tax has been 
introduced by major maritime nations such as Greece, Singapore, UK, 
Norway, etc., but not India. Moreover, this tonnage tax reduces the burden on 
ailing ships. It will not have any adverse impact on the revenue of the 
Government of India. According to a study conducted by TERI, if the tonnage 
tax is introduced in place of corporate tax,  in the next 10 ye ars, India will be 
able to add Rs. 5,135 cores to its cumulative GDP and Rs. 507.7 crores to its 
cumulative tax revenue. Hence, I strongly request the hon. Minister to pursue 
the matter with the Finance Ministry and immediately introduce tonnage tax for 
the revival of the shipping industry. 
Under clause 356 (g), you are appointing a surveyor to ensure that 
the ships are complied with the provisions of the Bill and to check the validity 
of international pollution prevention certificate, etc. But you have not specified 
any qualifications for him. I suggest t hat the surveyor so appointed should be 
a technical person, preferably a Marine Engineer, since he has to look into the 
technical and other aspects specified un der subclauses (a) to  (e) of this 
clause. 
Then under clause 356 (h) the D.G. is authorized to detain oil tankers 
and any other ship if they contravene the provisions. But the Bill is silent about 
the period of detention. The D.G. cannot detain any tanker or a ship beyond a 
reasonable period of time. It would have adverse ramifications in the maritime 
nations and thereby would affect our sh ipping business and also the image of 
the country. Therefore, I request the hon.  Minister to make it specific and the 
D.G. be mandated to complete all formalities or procedures within a 
prescribed period and release the ships and tankers in waters or send them 
back to the country from where they have come. 
Sir, these are a few issues which I thought of bringing to the notice of 
the hon. Minister. I would also request him to reply to my queries which I have 
raised.  Thank you. 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR (Tripura): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I rise to 
express my views on the Merchant Sh ipping (Amendment) Bill, 2003. It is 
written in the Statement of Objects and R easons that as an active member of 
the International Maritime Organisation, India has acceded to a number of 
International Conventions and Protocols adopted by the IMO.    I think    it 
268 

[30 July, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
should not have been done so late. They have given more stress on issuing of 
certificates. But the question of vigi lance has been avoided. They have not 
given much importance to how pollution occurs and how it can be stopped. I 
understand that this Bill is in consonan ce with the international laws which 
were established as early as in 1954 in UK. What are the objectives of these 
laws? The objectives are: (a) prevention of willful attempt of pollution in the sea 
by oil; and (b) prevention from subst ances coming from offshore industries. 
But these things are not there in t he Bill. Then there is no mention of 
minimisation of spoilage of oil, pr evention of shore generated waste, air 
pollution and poisonous gases, in the Bill. Sir, oil pollution is of a great concern 
to us because oil comes from the Middl e-East. It comes across the seas. It 
cannot come by air as it will be very costly. It cannot come by road also. So, 
oil pollution is a very important thing which needs to be looked into. Sir, our 
coastal line is a very long line. Some Members say that it is 5,700 kms. of 
length. I think, it is more  than that. It will exceed 6,000 kms. Along the coastal 
line, there are as many as 50 cities, most ly industrial; small and big cities are 
there. And, many rivers have terminated into the seas. All these rivers carry 
huge quantity of untreated sewage and all these industrial cities discharge 
waste materials into the rivers and into the seas. All these things together 
pose a threat to our environment. The ecological balances are disturbed by 
this. Now. all these spoils have not got importance in this Bill. 
I would like to point but another important matter. In India, we are 
having the largest ship-breaking yard which is at Alang near Bhavnagar in 
Gujarat. What happens there? When t he lifetime of the ships exceed 25-30 
years, these are sent to Alang by the capitalists or by persons having special 
interests. There the ships are broken an d steel is taken from the body of the 
ships. About 70 per cent of the replaceable ships of the whole world come 
here. Substances like polychlorinated bi phenyls, zinc, lead, inflammable oil 
products, explosives, etc. are brought to Alang for breaking these ships, and 
by this, the pollution is intensified. Now, this aspect has not been considered 
in this Amendment Bill. 
Sir, the Amendment Bill has been brought in line with the 
international laws and as per the Convention of the IMO. Since we are a 
member of the IMO, we have to abide by it.. But the thing is that we have to 
be alert. If our sea-shores are not free from pollution, or, say, if we cannot 
have them up to the international level, a call may come to India to 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2003] 
sell the shores, and these may go in the hands of the imperialists. This type of 
occupation may take place because we are in this LPG (liberalisation, 
privatisation and globalisation) syst em. In the present situation when 
everything is being privatised, -- even the Airways are going to be privatised -- 
I am afraid, we are going into the domain of the imperialists. Hence care 
should be taken and every effort should be taken to prevent such a thing from 
happening. With these words, Sir, I conclude. Thank you.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Price Policy for Kharif Crops of 2003-2004 Season. 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI RAJNATH SINGH): Sir, 
the Government has fixed the Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) for Fair 
Average Quality (FAQ) of Kharif Cr ops of 2003-2004 season. The MSP of 
paddy common and paddy Grade-A has been raised by Rs. 20 each as 
compared to the previous year and fixed at Rs. 550 and Rs. 580 per quintal 
respectively. 
The MSPs of Jowar, Bajra, Maize and Ragi have been raised by Rs. 
20 each and fixed at Rs. 505 per quintal as against Rs. 485 per quintal fixed 
for the previous year. 
The MSP of Arhar (Tur) has been raised to Rs. 1360 per quintal as 
against Rs. 1320 per quintal for the previous year, thus marking an increase 
of Rs. 40 per quintal. Similarly, the MSPs of Moong and Urad have been 
raised by "Rs. 40 per quintal as compared to the previous year. The Minimum 
Support Price of groundnut-in-shell has been fixed at Rs. 1400 per quintal 
marking an increase of Rs.-45-per Quinta l as compared to the last year.   
Similarly, the MSPs of soyabean (yellow) and soyabean (black) have

respectively. 
The MSP of sunflower seed has  been raised from Rs.1195 per 
quintal last year to Rs.1250 per quintal for the 2003-04 season, marking an 
increase of Rs.55 per quintal. 
As compared to the last year, the MSPs of sesamum and Nigerseed 
have been fixed at Rs. 1485 per quintal and Rs.1155 per quintal respectively 
marking an increase of Rs.35 per quintal. 
The MSP of cotton (F-414/H-777/J-34) and (H-4) varieties have been 
raised by Rs.50 per quintal as compared to the previous year. 
It is expected that the increases e ffected in the MSPs of the kharif 
crops will encourage the farmers for increasing the production and productivity 
of the crops in the country and will also encourage the farmers in 
diversification of crops.

Task force on employment generation 
*161. DR. A. R. KIDWAI: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Planning Commission has constituted another task force 
to identify sectors, sub-sectors and economic activities at the State level with a 
large potential for employment generation; 
(b) if so, whether Planning Commission has asked States to bring about 
reforms in labour laws for optimum utilisation of the resources available in 
order to create employment opportunities; 
(c) if so, to what extent this task force have been able to recommend the 
methodologies and procedures for the monitoring of employment and for 
gathering information; and 
(d) to what extent the target set for employment in the Tenth Plan would 
be fully met? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) The Planning Commission has 
set up a Task Force on formulation of State level employment strategy, 
monitoring employment generation at state level and implementation of the 
employment related programmes and policies in the Tenth Plan by the State 
Governments. The terms of reference of Task Force are specified in the Order 
of the Planning Commission placed as Statement. (See below) 
(b) Terms of reference of the Task Force do not include "reforms in labour 
laws". 
(c) The Task Force has been asked to submit its report by March, 2004. 
(d) The Government has not scaled down the target set for 
employment in the Tenth Plan.

and vocational training system; and (b) the labour hiring and 
manpower recruitment policies and procedures; so as to (i) 
reduce the mismatch between facilities for vocational training 
and demand for labour in the State; and (ii) to prepare the large 
number of 15+ youth passing out of schools at class VIII stage 
for gainful employment as and when they enter labour force. 
2.2.2 To suggest modalities for strengthening the link between 
vocational training and employment at State and district level, 
particularly for the youth and women in Rural Areas.

Liberal credit facilities for small units 
*162. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO:  Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether small enterprises are faci ng increased competition due to 
liberalized imports; 
(b) the steps contemplated for resolving problems being faced by them 
including global competition and liberalized imports; and 
(c) whether Government are considering grant of liberal credit facilities 
to small units as part of the steps proposed to be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCA LE INDUSTRIES (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR):(a) and (b) Liberalised imports due to the removal of Quantitative 
Restrictions (QRs) and reduction of tariff have exposed the SSI units to 
greater competition. However, even after the removal of QRs, protection to the 
industries is available in the form of raising customs duties upto the bound 
levels, imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards measures in case of 
surge in imports, etc. 
The Government has put in place seve ral measures to help SSIs become 
globally competitive. These include special focus on areas such as technology 
upgradation, infrastructure assist ance through cluster approach, timely 
availability of credit, adoption of modern management practices, use of 
electronic infrastructure and other IT applications to face the emerging 
challenges of trade liberalization. 
A comprehensive policy package for the development of SSIs announced 
on 30th August, 2000, serves to enhance the competitiveness of SSIs through 
easier access to credit, availability of collateral free composite loan upto Rs. 
25 lakhs, capital subsidy for technology upgradation and improved 
infrastructure. 
(c) Some of the steps taken by the Government relating to grant of liberal 
credit facilities to SSI sector are as under:— 
(i) As per the announcement made by the Finance Minister in the Union 
Budget 2003-04, the Indian Banks' Association has advised the 
banks to adopt the interest rate band of 2% above and below their 
prime lending rates for secured advances. 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2003] 
(ii) Banks have agreed to enhance the composite loan limit from Rs. 25 
lakhs to Rs. 50 lakhs for the SSIs. 
(iii) Ministry of SSI has identified 60 clusters for focused development 
of SSIs. The list of 60 clusters was sent by the Ministry of SSI to 
the RBI. RBI in turn has written to the commercial banks to 
formulate credit plans by incorpor ating the credit requirements of 
the SSI units in the State Credit Plans.

(b) Does not arise. 
(c) The main elements of the strategy for sustaining the growth of

(i)   Full exemption of the software and software services sector from 
licensing requirements. 
(ii)    100% exemption from payment of duties for software exports.

Software Exports.

Letter Rogatory: If, in the course of an investigation into an offence, an 
application is made by the investigating officer or any officer superior in rank 
to the investigating officer that eviden ce may be available in a country or 
place outside India, any cr iminal court may issue a Letter Rogatory/letter of 
request to a court or any authority in that country or place competent to deal 
with such request to examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with 
facts and circumstances of the case and to record his statement made in the 
course of such examination and also to require such person or any other 
person to produce any document or thing which may be in his possession 
pertaining to the case and to forward all the evidence so taken or collected or 
the authenticated copies thereof or the thing so collected to the court issuing 
such letter. Letters Rogatory/letters of request are issued to obtain evidence 
required in investigation of criminal cases and not used for extradition of 
fugitive offenders. Although, the instrument of request is referred generally as 
a letter rogatory", the terms "letter rogatory" and "letter of request" (which is 
used specifically in the Hague Evidence Convention) have come to be 
virtually synonymous in actual practice. 
Government has sent 120 letters Rogatory to foreign countries during the 
last five years as per following details: 1997—27,2000—24, 2001—
25,2002—18, and 2003 (upto June)-16. 
Similarly, Government has received 326 letters rogatory from foreign 
countries as per following details: 1999-73, 2000—62, 2001—74, 2002—56,

Exposure of workers to radiation 
1185. SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether workers of Kalpakkam Atomic Reprocessing Plant were over-
exposed to high radiation; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the steps being taken as safety measures to avoid such incidents in 
future; 
(d) whether the victims can continue with the present job after this 
incident; and 
(e) whether Government would provide any compensation to the victims 
taking into account the damage caused to their lives? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) Yes, Sir. There has 
been an incident of over-exposure of six persons at the Kalpakkam 
Reprocessing Plant (KARP) on January 21, 2003. 
(b) On January 21, 2003, when the Reprocessing Plant was under normal 
operation, there was an incident of inadvertent over-exposure to radiation of 
six persons during the process of transfer of low level liquid waste from a 
tank in an area, away from the main Reprocessing Plant. The cause of the 
incident, as identified later on by a specially constituted Technical Committee, 
was a minor leak in an isolation valve 
54 

[31 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
separating a high level liquid waste tank from the low level liquid waste tank 
resulting in increase in activity level in the latter. Since the leak was of a 
minor nature, it had gone unnoticed by the persons involved in the transfer of 
liquid waste. This was noticed when a sample of the low level liquid waste 
which was being transferred showed a higher than expected level of 
radioactivity. As a result, the six personnel who were involved in this transfer 
operation were inadvertently exposed to higher than the annual dose limit. The 
safety authorities have investigated the incident according to the procedure, 
which involves measurement of radiation doses received, establishing the 
root cause and medical examination of  the exposed personnel. The Medical 
Authorities have certified that all these six personnel are in good health and 
there were no abnormal findings. There was neither any release of 
radioactivity to the environment nor any risk of exposure to any member of the 
public. 
(c) Bhaba Atomic Research Centre has well laid out mechanisms to 
review the safety status of Operating Plants. As per prevailing practice, the 
facility was immediately shutdown and an independent Technical Committee 
was set up to investigate the abnormal incident, so that remedial measures 
could be taken to prevent such recurrence and to disseminate the lessons 
learnt to other similar fac ilities. BARC are implementing the 
recommendations of the Technical Committee. 
(d) Yes, Sir. Since these personnel involved are physically fit and are in 
good health with no adverse symptoms, they are quite capable to continue to 
work in the Reprocessing Plant. However, as per the prevailing Safety 
Guidelines followed at BARC, these persons have been assigned jobs in the non-
radioactive areas. 
(e) In view of the fact that the medi cal report certifies that the persons 
involved are in good health, the question of compensation does not arise.

MAHARIA): (a) and (b) Foodgrains of fair average quality conforming to the 
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) standards are distributed under 
Public Distribution System (PDS). 
A few complaints about the quality of foodgrains supplied under the PDS 
were received during the last three years. 
During 2000-2001, co mplaints were received from the State 
Governments of Arunachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, Sikkim 
and Tripura regarding supply of foodgrains of poor quality, especially rice 
procured under relaxed specifications (URS). Keeping in view the reluctance 
of consumers, the supply of URS rice of 1997-98 Kharif Marketing Season 
was stopped. 
During 2001-2002, the Governments of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Rajasthan and NCT of Delhi complained about the supply of 
"lustre lost" wheat while the Governments of Goa and Kerala complained 
about the poor quality of rice stocks. It was explained to the State Governments 
that, except in appearance,  lustre lost wheat is as good as sound wheat, 
especially in terms of nutritional value. The FCI officers were instructed to 
ensure that rice of good quality only was supplied under the PDS to Goa and 
Kerala. 
During 2002-2003, the Governments of Rajasthan, Delhi, Gujarat and 
Maharashtra had complained about issue of poor quality of "lustre lost" wheat 
under PDS and Government of Karnataka and Kerala had complained about the 
issue of poor quality of rice under various schemes. Keeping in view the 
reluctance of consumers, the issue of "lustre lost" wheat for distribution under 
TPDS was stopped. FCI was instructed to ensure that rice of good quality 
only is supplied under the PDS in Karnataka and Kerala. 
No complaint has been received fr om any State during this year 
regarding supply of poor quality rice and wheat by FCI under PDS. 
The State Governments are free to inspect the stocks of foodgrains and 
satisfy themselves about their quality before lifting the same from FCI depots. 
The States Governments have also been advised to depute an officer not below 
the rank of Inspector to check the quality of stocks.

Cases of Diplomatic Immunity 
  1254.    SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
SHRI JIBON ROY: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Diplomatic Immunity under the 
Vienna Convention was granted to diplomats so that they are not harassed 
unnecessarily; 
(b) if so, the reasons for diplomatic immunity in three cases involving 
Zimbabwean diplomat's car, another diplomat's wife slapping a senior 
journalist and Senegalese Ambassador's son killing his father's driver in a 
scuffle; and 
(c) if so, what steps are being taken to book such culprits? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) Yes. 
(b) Under Article 31 of Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 
1961, a diplomatic agent enjoys immunity from 'Criminal Jurisdiction' of the 
receiving state. Article 37 extends this immunity to the members of the family 
of a diplomatic agent forming part of his household, provided they are not 
nationals of the receiving state. India is a party to the Vienna Convention and 
has ratified this convention on 15th October, 1965. In order to give effect to 
this convention, the Parliament enacted the Diplomatic Relations (Vienna 
Convention) Act, 1972 to have the force of law. Under the provisions of this 
Act of Parliament, it is obligatory 
129 

RAJYA  SABHA [31 July, 2003] 
on the part of Government of India to provide diplomatic immunity to 
diplomats and their family members unless it is waived by the sending state 
on the request of the Government of India, as per Article 32 of the Vienna 
Convention. 
(c) In line with Article 31 (4) of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic 
Relations, 1961, the immunity of a diplomatic agent from the jurisdiction of the 
receiving state does not exempt him from the jurisdiction of the sending state. 
The Government of India requested the Government of Senegal for trial of 
Mr. Mansoor Ali, son of the Ambassador of Senegal for culpable homicide 
not amounting to murder under their local laws. The Senegalese Govt. 
exercising its sovereign prerogative recalled the Ambassador & family. In the 
other two cases, the need for waiver of diplomatic immunity or trial of 
diplomats concerned did not arise as no specific charges could be framed by 
the police against them.

1277. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state:

from being employed in hazardous occupations;

labour force in the country; and

SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) Yes, Sir. 
147

(b) The Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986 prohibits 
employment of children below the age of 14 years in 13 Occupations & 57 
Processes listed in the schedule to the Act. 
(c) Occupations and processes listed in the schedule to the Act are 
considered hazardous for the purpose of prohibiting employment of children. 
(d) and (e) The Government has alread y formulated a National Policy on 
Child Labour, 1987 which consists of the following three components: 
(i) A legislative action Plan 
(ii) Focussing of general development programmes for benefiting child

running special schools/centres for rehabilitation of children withdrawn from 
work through non-formal/formal education, vocational training, nutrition, 
health care, stipend etc. So far, 100 NCLPs are under implementation in13

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) Authentic information on child labour is 
generated by the decennial census. According to the 1991 census, the number 
of working children in the State of Orissa is 4,52,394. Figures of the 2001

schools.

(a) whether it is a fact that Madhya Pradesh has been provided Central 
assistance to the tune of Rs.9324.31 crores under Ninth Five Year Plan and 
Rs. 10168.13 crores have been estimated to be provided during the Tenth Five 
Year Plan; 
(b) the names of such States which ha ve been projected to be provided 
more than Rs.4000 crores as Central assistance during Tenth Five Year Plan as 
compared to the Ninth Five Year Plan; 
(c) the details of the additional amount projected to be provided to these 
States together with the basis thereof; and 
(d) the details of the criteria for providing Central assistance to the States 
and whether Central assistance has also been provided by deviating from 
these criteria? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) The total Central Assistance 
(CA) allocated to the State of Madhy a Pradesh during the Ninth Plan is 
Rs.9324.32 crore and the corresponding projection for Tenth Plan is Rs. 
10168.13 crore. 
(b) The States which have been projected to be provided more than Rs. 
4000 crore as central assi stance during Tenth Five Year Plan as compared to 
the Ninth Five Year Plan are: Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh. 
(c) and (d) The allocation of Central Assistance for the Annual Plans of 
States are based on the overall resource availability of the Centre and the 
gross budgetary support for Plan. The Central Assistance for the Annual Plans 
of States comprises of Normal Central Assistance (NCA), Additional Central 
Assistance (ACA) for externally Aided Projects (EAPs) and ACA for Special 
and Other Programmes. While allocation of NCA is based on the Gadgil 
Formula as approved by the National Development Council (NDC) in 
December, 1991, allocation of the ACA for EAPs and ACA for Special and 
Other Programmes are based on the

178

done by the State Governments themselves as per their own priorities and the

support is mainly for activities like data collection, ground water exploration,

Resources have allocated Rs. 85 crores in the Tenth Plan for the National 
Water Development Agency for investigation work on interlinking of rivers.

Credit support to farmers 
1303. DR. DASARI NARAYANA R AO: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any action plan for 
implementation during the Tenth Five Year Plan for providing timely and 
179 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2003] 
adequate credit support to farmers particularly to small and marginal farmers; 
and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and (b) The Government of 
India has initiated various policy measures to improve the access of farmers to 
institutional sources of credit. The emphasis of these policies has continued to 
be on progressive institutionalisation for providing timely and adequate credit 
support to farmers with particular focus on small and marginal farmers and 
weaker sections of societ y to enable them to adopt modern technology and 
improved agricultural practices for increasing agricultural production and 
productivity. 
2. Some of the important measures that have been or are being taken to 
provide increased flow of credit to the agriculture sector are as under: 
* The instrument of Kisan Credit Scheme (KCC) has been 
introduced to provide timely credit support from the banking 
system to the farmers for cultivation needs including purchase of 
inputs in a flexible and cost effective manner. As on 31st March, 
2003, cumulatively 313.44 lakh KCCs involving sanctioned bank 
loan of Rs. 76,498.80 crore we re issued to the farmers by 
Cooperative Banks, Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Commercial 
Banks. Personal Accident Insurance Scheme was formulated for 
KCC holders to cover them against accidental death/personal 
disability. 
* A Supplementary credit delivery mechanism through Self Help 
Groups (SHGs) assimilating the flexibility and responsiveness of the 
informal sector with resources and network of the banking system 
has become an integral part of the rural financial infrastructure 
providing financial services to the poor in a sustainable manner. 
Upto 31st March, 2003. 7.17 lakh SHGs have been formed 
covering an estimated number of 1.16 crore families. Cumulatively, 
banks have provided financial assistance of Rs. 2043 crore to the 
SHGs and NABARD has extended refinance assistance of Rs. 
1419 crore. During the year 2002-03, bank finance to SHGs was of 
the order of Rs. 1022. 33 crore with NABARD refinance of Rs. 
622.33 crore. 
180 

[31 July, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
3. In addition, large number of credit linked subsidy schemes are also 
under implementation. 
4. As per NABARD, the total quantum of ground level credit flow for 
agriculture and allied activities provided by Cooperative Banks, Commercial Banks, 
RRBs and other agencies increased from Rs. 62,045 crore during 2001-02 to an 
estimated level of Rs. 75,000 crore in 2002-03 this is further expected to increase 
on yearly basis during Tenth Plan. 
5. With a view to strengthening the flow of credit to small and marginal 
farmers, relaxations in regard to marg in money requirements, security norms 
etc. have been extended to such borrowers.

1326. SHRI RUMANDLA RAAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the Minister 
of SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Small Scale Industry Units often complaint about the 
prevalence of Inspector Raj harassing them on plea of safety, security and 
environment; and 
(b) if so, the remedial measures proposed to check their harassment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR):  (a) and (b) Government have 
occasionally received representations fr om industry associ ations and Small 
Scale Industries (SSI) units about the prevalence of Inspector Raj. 
Government have already introduced a system of inspection based on selection 
of units from defaulters list in the Employees Provident Fund Organization 
(EPFO) and Employees State Insurance Corporation (ESIC). In addition, 
Government have recommended to all the State Governments that they 
consider putting in place of self-Cer tification System wherein returns 
submitted on various labour laws by small scale units are certified and this may 
be treated as prima facie compliance. Under this system inspections would be 
conducted only when essential i.e. on receipt of written, verifiable and signed 
complaints from stakeholders. 
Government had also entrusted a study for simplification of laws, rules 
and procedures affecting the SSI sector to the Administrative Staff College of 
India (ASCI). The draft of a Small En terprises Development Bill received

Increase in quantum of advances to SSI 
1327. SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the quantum  of advances to SSI sector have 
increased during the last year in spite of industrial slump; 
(b) whether the quantum of credit flow to the SSI sector is adequate to 
meet the requirements of the funds for SSI sector in the year 2002-03; and 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [31 July, 2003] 
(c) the efforts that are being made or proposed to be made in future by 
Government to improve the situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) and (b) The advances to Small 
Scale Industrial (SSI) Sector from Public  Sector Banks during last year have 
increased from Rs. 49,743 crores as at the end of March, 2002 to Rs. 52,988 
crores as at the end of March, 2003. However, the share of credit to SSI sector 
in the Net Bank Credit has declined from 12.5% in March, 2002 to 11.1 % in 
March, 2003. In the context of target of growth in the SSI Sector, the quantum 
of credit flow cannot be considered as adequate. 
(c) Government took up the issue of improving credit flow to SSI Sector 
with Reserve Bank of India (RBI) through its Standing Advisory Committee 
to Review the Flow of Institutional Credit to SSI sector. Based on the 
recommendations of the Standing Advisory Committee, Government has 
taken various new important decisions relating to credit facilities to SSI Sector. 
Some of the decisions are as under:— 
(i) As per the announcement made by the Finance Minister in the 
Union Budget 2003-04, the Indian Banks' Association has advised 
the banks to adopt the interest rate band of 2% above and below their 
prime lending rates for secured advances. 
(ii) Banks have agreed to enhance composite loan limit from Rs. 25 
lakhs to Rs. 50 lakhs for the SSIs. 
(iii) Ministry of SSI has identified 60 clusters for focused development 
of SSIs. The list of 60 clusters was sent by the Ministry of SSI to 
the RBI. RBI in turn has written to the commercial banks to 
formulate credit plans by incorporating SSIs' credit requirement in 
the States Credit Plans. 
(iv) Credit Guarantee Trust Fund for Small Industries to review its 
decisions in respect of loans upto Rs. 5 lakhs.

Development of cryogenic engine 
t1329. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the present status of development of cryogenic engine being 
developed by indigenous technique for space programme; 
(b) by when the Indian satellite, based on indigenous cryogenic engine, 
is expected to be launched at first; and 
(c) whether the indigenously developed cryogenic engines would be 
sold to other countries also? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE) : (a) The indigenous cryogenic 
engine has been evaluated in a number of ground hot firing tests for a 
cumulative duration of about 4000 seconds using two sets of engine 
hardware. This included the intended full flight duration for 700 seconds. 
Preparations have been made for the development and qualification of the 
integrated indigenous cryogenic stage, including the engine by early 2004. 
(b) The first flight demonstration of the indigenous cryogenic upper stage 
is tentatively planned during 2004-05 based on a success-oriented schedule for 
the qualification of the indigenous stage. 
(c) There are no such plans at present.

PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ (Jammu and Kashmir): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, there is no scope for a longer speech on this Bill. But I have to 
say a couple of things. Luckily, today, the hon. Minster has to give some 
clarifications. Some Members would get some time, then. But, here I wanted to 
point out that the hon. Minister has suggested a penalty of Rs. 250 for the 
ticket-less passengers. But I would say it should be Rs. 500 or the fare of the 
distance, intended to be travelled by the offender. Suppose a ticket-less 
person wants to' go to Chennai, the natural justice that this Bill could provide 
is, he should be charged the fare for Chennai or Rs. 500, whichever is more. 
Or, if the hon. Minister wants to be very  sympathetic, it could be 'whichever is 
less'. But the 'distance intended to be covered by the offender' should be the 
barometer for fixing the penalty. Despite the fact that I rate the hon. Minister as 
a capable person, I would like to share my feelings with the House that the 
Railway Department is in a shambles . There are many measures which the 
hon. Minister cannot take up because there is no money. Railways have 
substantial money, but st ill they want more money for security purpose, for 
providing a safe journey to its passengers, and for modernization. This 
Department has substantial resources, but even with all those resources, they 
are short of funds. Therefore, moderniza tion has not taken place at the pace I 
wanted, at the pace hon. Members w anted. So, modernization, ensuring 
perfect security and the safety of passengers is the need of the hour. Madam, I 
can share my feelings with you. People are, now, scared to travel by train. 
People, who can afford to travel by air, travel by air, but the poor people are 
compelled to travel by train. But the question of railway safety is a very broad 
one, which is before the people of our country. Those questions will definitely 
come up. Therefore, I would like, the hon.  Minister to raise resources to make 
railway travel safe and secure. At the sa me time he should also think in terms 
of modernizing Railways. Country is crying for that. If there is an offender, 
there is no question of showing any sympathy towards him or her. Whosoever 
travels by train, he must feel secure d; he must feel comfortable. When you 
travel by train, you will find there are no tissue papers available even in the AC 
(I Class); there is no soap. Even a hanger to hang your clothes would be 
provided only when you will demand for that.   This is the state of affairs in the 
AC (I Class).    You can very well

imagine what would be the situation in other classes. Nothing is available 
there. Railway bogies are in a shambles. You need a lot of funds for 
modernization, for security, for the safety of passengers. Ninety-eight per cent

Minister, Mr. Nitish Kumar, has a great responsibility on his shoulders. So far 
as accidents are concerned, I would come to it later on. But, here, I would only 
like to say that he must raise money.  There is no question of showing any 
sympathy towards ticket-less passengers. Whosoever travels by train, he must 
pay. Therefore, laws, in this regard, have to be very stringent. I would like to

Then, I have not brought in the realm of this Bill, that is, the

corruption. It is not only a question of ti cketless travellers, but there are people 
who pay extra money to get reservations  done. He must modernize Railways 
wholly and while doing so he must tackle corruption.

Madam, the hon. Minister has brought fo rward this Bill to amend sections 137 
and 138. Though it appears to be a small amendment, I would like to put 
some questions to the hon. Minister si nce it will have a lot of impact on the 
passengers who travel by trains. 
Madam, there are two types of offe nders. There are wilful offenders 
and habitual offenders. The railway authorities should concentrate on 
professional manipulators who collect money at one point and, then, help 
passengers in travelling without tickets in the trains. They are called wilful 
manipulators. These are the persons responsible for causing loss to the 
Railways. The Railway authorities should concentrate on such people. And, at 
times, while coming to station, there is every possibility of bona fide travellers, 
unknowingly, boarding a wrong train at wrong place. So, there should be 
some mention about the people who are travelling in a bona fide manner and 
there should be some differentiation between the wilful offenders and the 
habitual offenders. I want to know from  the hon. Minister -- since for the past 
five years the number of ticketless passenge rs is increasing year after year -- 
what are the figures for the past five years? Are they on the increase or on the 
decrease? How much amount has been co llected from them by way of fines? 
How many people have been sentenced to jail?   How many people have 
been punished?   I would also

SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY (West Bengal): Madam, while speaking 
on the Railways (Amendment) Bill, 2003, which has been brought forward to 
amend the Railways Act, 1989, I would like to raise some relevant points. 
Madam, in the Statement of Objects and Reasons, it has been stated 
that "...proposed to increase the mi nimum penalty for ticketless travel 
specified in sub-section (3 ) of section 137 and sub-section (3) of section 138 
from fifty rupees to two hundred and fifty rupees which was expected to 
minimize the inconvenience to the genu ine passengers by deterring ticketless 
or irregular travellers." This concern for the genuine passengers is quite 
justified as there are a number of passeng ers who can afford rail fare but still 
travel without ticket, or, travel beyond authorized journey. These travellers 
create inconvenience for the genuine passengers and this should be stopped 
forthwith. 
Though this step has been described as an effort to "... minimise the 
inconvenience to the genuine passengers by deterring ticketless or irregular 
travellers", the Ministry should ensur e that genuine passengers are also not 
deprived of other amenities which they are entitled to while travelling. The 
Government should also keep in mind the fact that in our country a good 
number of people belong to the Below Poverty Line and cannot afford to buy 
rail tickets. Over the years, rail fares have also increased quite a lot, making it 
even more difficult for them to buy tickets. If the Ministry is really serious about 
it and wants to make more and more people buy rail tickets, rail fares should 
be reduced so that it remains within the reach of the poor. That would ensure 
more buyers for railway tickets and would reduce the number of passengers 
travelling without tickets. And, the Mi nistry should also ensure that the 
increase in penalty does not become an extra burden on the poor, ticketless 
travellers.

Need for fixing Minimum Support Price for Oilpalm to safeguard the interests 
of the Oilpalm-growing farmers in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, the State of Andhra Pradesh has done pioneering work in 
oilpalm cultivation accounting for 59 per cent of the total oilpalm plantations in 
the country. As the Market Interventi on Scheme, which is being implemented 
in the State, could not give confidenc e to the farmers that they would get 
remunerative prices, the necessity for announcing the Minimum Support Price 
(MSP) was categorically brought to the not ice of the Governm ent of India. In 
this regard, two proposals in respect of the modalities to be followed for 
implementing the MSP for oilpalm were considered, namely:- 
The procuring agency could buy fres h fruit bunches of oilpalm, get 
them crushed on agency basis and sell crude palm oil at the 
appropriate time. 
Alternatively, the procuring agency could buy crude palm oil. 
After considering these two proposals, it was decided that the first 
proposal would be more beneficial. In  view of the facts mentioned above, I 
would seek the intervention of the Go vernment of India and request it to 
announce the Minimum Support Price for oilpalm to safeguard the interests of 
the oilpalm-growing farmers in the State from the price fluctuations of crude 
palm oil. This will also encourage our farmers to undertake larger cultivation of 
oilpalm which would help us to tide ov er our acute shortage of edible oil and 
reduce our dependence on its import and thereby save our forex reserves.   
Thank you, Madam. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY) in the Chair]

SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY (West B engal): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir. 
the Farakka bridge on the river Ganga is strategically located and is the only 
link between the North-East and the rest of the country. The National Highway 
No. 34 also passes through the bridge and it is also linked with Nathu-La at 
the Indo-China border.

loading vehicles is not reduced soon.

Government a number of times for constructing a second bridge. There was a 
provision of second bridge on the river Ganga when the existing bridge was 
constructed. But the Centre has rejected the proposal which would cost nearly 
Rs. 120 crores, for want of funds.

issue has been raised a number of time s in the House, but the Government 
has not yet taken any action in this regard. Construction of a second bridge is 
not merely a local demand, it is al so important from  defence and national 
security aspects. So, keeping all these things in mind, l urge upon the Central 
Government to repair the existing bridge and construct a second bridge 
immediately.   Thank you. 
Crisis in the tea plantation sector 
SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala): Mr. vice-Chairman, Sir, the 
tea plantation sector in the country is facing a serious crisis. Many tea 
plantations in various parts of the country have been closed and many are on 
the verge of closure. Lakhs of labour ers have lost their livelihood and many 
are on the brink of retrenchment. Near famine conditions exist in many of the 
labour settlements with many starvation deaths reported from different parts of 
the country. 
The decision of the Central Govern ment to remove the quantitative 
restrictions on imports even of agricul tural produces has paved the way for 
uncontrolled and large-scale import of te a from other countries. The tri-party 
agreement between the SAARC countries allowing manufacturers to import 
tea and a very low import duty has further aggravated the situation.    The

Need to stop Pampa and Achancoil Vaipar Link Project 
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Keral a): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
despite strong protests from the Kera la Government and ecologists against 
the movement to divert water from Pampa and Achancoil rivers, the Union 
Government appears to be determined to implement the proposed Pampa 
Achancoil Vaipar Link Project. The construction of Mekkara Dam for the 
storage of water to be diverted from Pampa and Achancoil rivers is also 
completed. The National Water Development Agency also favours the said 
project. The proposed project is on the bas is of a feasibility report prepared by 
the National Water Development Agen cy, (NWDA). The Centre for Water 
Resources Development and Management had also conducted a detailed 
study on the quantity of water requirements in the Pampa Achancoil rivers and 
found that there is no surplus water to be diverted. This is contrary to the view 
of the NWDA. The Pampa and the Achancoil Rivers are the lifelines of 
Vembanad Kol wetlands and if the proj ect is implemented, it would ruin the 
wetland ecology of Kerala. The Vembanad Kol wetland is the largest tropical 
wetland eco system in the South-West  Coast of India. Any movement to 
implement the diversion proposal would lead to submerging of thousands of 
acres of forest land and render the Central Travancore Districts drought-prone. 
Therefore, it is urged that the Government should review the water 
diversion proposal and drop the movement to interlink the Pampa, Achancoil

Need for reviewing the provisions of Dowry Prohibition Act 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): The word 'dowry' is almost 
synonymous with women's oppression. It is one of the causes for the low 
status of women. The hi gh cost of marriage makes things difficult for the 
parents of women, and it is a source of lucre for their marital families. 
There is ample evidence that the phenomenon of dowry is expanding 
and the value of dowry is rising to untenable limits. There are horrific reports of 
-fathers selling kidneys to cover dowry payment or of collective suicides in 
families with many daughters. T he Department of Women and Child 
Development had reported that there were 6,006 dowry deaths in 1997. 
Legal drives to ban the practice of dowry in India have met with little 
success. The Dowry Prohibition (Ame ndment) Act, (1984 & 1986) makes the 
giving and taking of dowry 'as a condition of marriage' punishable by law, 
while it excluded 'voluntary gifts', which reduced the provisions to toothless 
sanctions. 
The Indian women's movement has advocated changes on a broader 
level, both in the context of gender subordination and social changes in 
attitudes towards daughters. The sad side  of our national life today is that 
giving and taking of dowry is an accepted practice. Everybody does it. Some 
cases which go reported, like that of Nisha Sharma, do shake things up. But it 
is momentary. There are ripples in the water but soon water gets still again. 
The Government should get serious thought to this and should 
review the existing provisions in order to bring out  stringent penalties to act as 
a deterrent both for giving and accepting of dowry in any form.

with this Special Mention.

Request to retain Vettuva community of Kerala in SC/ST list 
SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, the Vettuvas of  the 
Malabar and Cochin areas of Kerala belong to the socially and economically 
backward community. They are traditional agricultural labourers engaged in 
coconut plucking. They have been included in the SC/ST list since 
Independence. Now, it is learnt that  the Central Government has taken a 
decision to exclude this community from the SC/ST list. It is very unfortunate 
that through this decision the Government has excluded the Vettuvas residing 
in three districts, namely, Trichur, Malappuram and Calicut, from the SC list, 
while the same community in the Southern Kerala has been retained as the 
Scheduled Castes. This discrimination will further worsen the uplift of the 
socially and economically backward sections in the Kerala society. Excepting 
a few families, the remaining Vettuvas are living in a very backward condition. 
I, therefore, urge upon the Govern ment to cancel the decision of 
excluding the Vettuvas from the SC list, and  to give necessary instructions to 
include them in the SC/ST list so that they are able to retain the benefits as 
envisaged in the Reservation Policy.

SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Sir, I am extremely 
pained and anguished to draw the attention of this august House regarding 
the most deplorable plight of  millions of the poor tribal  people in the country,

Parliamentarian like me. It was a stark revelation of facts that lakhs of poor

Supreme Court judgments on sanctuaries, or reserved forests or for 
constructing big dams, industries or mining. In fact, our experience shows

rehabilitated in right earnest since early fifties. Not even the benefit sharing 
with the communities could be a reality. The existing situation with the project-
affected families of the Sardar Sarovar Project is also an issue of very serious 
concern.

immediate attention of all right thinking people to find out a proper solution. No

you, I would also like to impress upon the Government that there should be a

country may collapse from within. I am afraid, unless the situation prevailing 
with the tribals, and millions of tribal people, are taken care of expressly, we 
shall be leading to a situation of no return.

Effect of Industrial discharge on ground water in Hyderabad 
*181. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Scientists of Acha rya N.G. Ranga Agricultural 
University, Andhra Pradesh, have foun d in a study that indiscriminate 
disposal of effluents from indust rial complexes in Hyderabad is 
affecting the quality of ground water; and 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to send a team to see 
the seriousness of situation and prov ide assistance in the setting up 
of treatment plants? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRO NMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI 
T.R. BAALU): (a) The findings of t he study carried out in 1997 at 
Acharya N.G. Ranga Agricultural University, Andhra Pradesh on "Soil 
and Water Resource characteristics in relation to Land Disposal of 
Industrial Effluents in Kattedan Industrial Development Area" revealed 
that ground water in the area is contaminated due to discharge of 
effluents from the industries located in Kattedan Industrial 
Development Area. 
(b) Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board has taken action 
against defaulting Industries located in Kattedan Industrial Area. As a 
result, most of the industries hav e upgraded pollution control systems 
and adopted cleaner production technologies.

to make an assessment of production during 2003-04. Besides 
contingency crop planning, efforts are also being made to promote 
varietal replacement and propagat ion of newer location specific 
High Yielding Varieties with biotic and abiotic resistance, efficient 
use of fertilizers and need-based plant protection measures.

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the number of foreign universities that are operating

[1 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Statement 
(a) and (b) A recent study of three leading newspapers in which 
advertisements of foreign universities were published, conducted by 
National Institute of Education Planning and Administration (NIEPA), 
revealed that 50 universities of USA, 39 universities of UK, 26 
universities of Australia and 7 universities of New Zealand are 
marketing their programmes in Indi a. Various types of arrangements 
ranging from franchise, tie-ups, twinning to external campus are on 
offer. 
According to an earlier survey, A ssociation of Indian Universities 
(AIU), scanned 14 national newspaper s over a six-month period (1st 
July-31st Dec 2000) for advertis ements, by foreign education 
providers, related to higher education opportunities. According to this 
survey, 144 foreign universities/coll eges/institutions were offering 
various courses of study to the Indian students. Out of them 117 
offered programmes on their home campuses and the remaining 27 
were conducting programmes in Indi a through their Indian partners. 
The largest number of these instit utions were from UK (53) and 
Australia (40) followed by USA (24), Canada (7) and New Zealand (5). 
The remaining institutions were from various other countries like 
Bulgaria, Cyprus, Hong Kong, Fr ance, Ireland, Mauritius, Nepal, 
Russia and Switzerland. 
The University Grants Commission (UGC) has proposed 
regulations for entry and operation of  foreign universities/educational 
institutions in India and necessary amendments to the UGC Act are 
under consideration of Government. 
However, All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) has 
issued Regulations for entry and operation of foreign universities/ 
institutions in India imparting technical education. According to these 
regulations "no foreign university/institution shall establish/operate its 
educational activity in India leading to award of diplomas/degrees 
including post-graduate and doctoral without the express permission/ 
approval of the Council". Further, any  Application for registration of 
foreign universities/institutions imparting/intending to impart technical 
education in India shall be inter-alia accompanied with the No 
objection certificate from the concerned  Embassy in  India,

Accreditation certificate of the fore ign university/institution by the 
authorised agency in the parent country and an undertaking from the 
foreign university/institution stating that the degree/diplomas awarded 
to the students in India is recognised in the parent country etc.

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT

Statement 
(a) to (d) As per the data furnished by National Crime Records 
Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs, dowry related incidents 
have shown an overall decline in the last five years. However, the 
incidence of dowry deaths in the four metropolitan cities of Chennai, 
Delhi, Kolkata and Mumbai was 121 in 2001 and 181 in 2002 
(provisional figures). State-wise number of dowry deaths in 2001 and 
2002 is as shown in Statement-I ( See below). Charge sheets were 
filed in 5952 cases of Dowry Deaths in 2000 and 6060 cases in 2001. 
(e) The Law Commission of India has recommended speedy trial 
by empowering the Investigative A gency, better coordination between 
investigating agencies and prosecutors, appointment of women public 
prosecutors, reducing holidays of the courts etc. 
Besides, Minister of Law and Justice has, in his recent letter to 
all the Chief Ministers and the Chie f Justice of the High Courts, urged 
to make immediate administrative arrangements to provide required 
relief to, inter-alia, women victims of sexual abuse and cruelty in 
marriage. He has also urged that wherever there is more than one fast 
Track Court in a District, one of these be earmarked to deal 
exclusively with cases of sexual abuse and cruelty in marriage relating 
to women.

Survival of Marine creatures 
*195. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the number of Marine creatures is 
slowly declining due to increasing salinity of water; 
(b) whether it is also a fact t hat the sea is not getting its due 
share of fresh water from its rivers, which helped to maintain the 
salinity at certain level for the survival of Marine creatures, and 
(c) if so, what steps Government propose to take for the survival 
of Marine creatures? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRO NMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI 
T.R. BAALU): (a) to (c) No Sir. As per the available information, there 
is no conclusive evidence regarding decline in number of marine 
creatures due to change in the level of salinity of water or flow of river

protection of marine organisms like enactment of the Wild Life 
(Protection) Act. 1972. establishment of marine National Parks, 
regulation of Coastal Zone and Biosphere Reserves.

†1333.   SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH 'LALAN': 
SHRI LAJPAT RAI: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that huge amount of subsidy being given 
to the farmers in the developed countries of the world is adversely 
affecting Indian agriculture products; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether Government have made any effort in this regard 
under WTO during the last years; and 
(d) if so, the details of such efforts, when they were made and 
the outcome thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HU KUMDEO NARAYAN YA DAV): (a) and (b) 
The continued high level of domestic support and export subsidies 
given to the farmers in the developed countries denies meaningful 
market access to the developing countries and depresses the 
international prices of subsidized agricultural products. In order to 
ensure that Indian farmers are not put to any hardship, the 
Government have put in place a suitable mechanism for monitoring the 
imports of sensitive items and are committed to providing adequate 
protection to the Indian farmers through various measures, including 
appropriate calibrations of applied tariffs within bound levels, recourse 
to trade remedies, and Government support consistent with World 
Trade Organization (W.T.O.).

proposals as well as co-sponsored proposals with like minded 
members of W.T.O. In these negotia ting proposals, India has sought, 
inter alia, substantial reduction in all forms of domestic support by the 
developed countries and elimination of export countries, except the 
export subsidies provided by the devel oping countries to reduce their 
high costs of marketing, including handling, upgrading and other 
processing costs and costs of transport and freight, permitted under 
the existing provisions of W.T.O. (Agreement on Agriculture) which 
would remain without reduction commitments. India has also proposed 
that food and livelihood security conc erns of the developing countries 
should be safeguarded, and substantial improvements in market 
access in products of export interest to developing countries should be 
agreed. The negotiations are scheduled to be concluded by 1st 
January, 2005.

diesel valued at Rs. 1020 crore per annum for around 45 
years after the stabilization of the yield (after 4-5 years). This

Deletion of spurious BT Cotton seeds 
1344. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA : Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Ce ntral Institute for Cotton Research 
has developed a kit which helps in detecting spurious Bt Cotton 
seeds; 
(b) if so, the details of the research; and 
(c) how it exactly helps the illiterate farmers in detecting 
spurious Bt Cotton seeds? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) Four kits have been developed to help the detection of 
spurious Bt. Seeds. Three kits (Bt- express, Bt-Quant and Bt-detect) 
are based on immunoassays and the fourth kit is through PCR-DNA. 
(c) The test can be done in the field or at home on seeds, leaf, 
stem on any tissue of the plant. The Bt-express kit contains Bt-express 
strips, plastic vials containing buffer, a plastic pestle and pictorial 
instructions. For detection in the seed, the seed has to be crushed and 
seed coat has to be discarded. The white cotyledons are to be placed 
into a vial containing buffer and crushed well. The Bt-express strip is 
placed in the vial (dipping the green end  of the strip into the solution). 
After 5 minutes, two purple coloured bands will appear if it is Bt-seed 
and only one band will appear if it is non-Bt type.

Use of Pesticides 
1348. SHRI R. KAMARAJ: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that pesticides 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [1 A ugust, 2003] 
abuse in our country is above 97000 tonnes and it is playing havoc 
with public life; 
(b) if so, the action taken by Government to avoid such 
impending danger; 
(c) whether Government have formulated any guidelines to check 
abuse of pesticides by keeping the same minimum residual level 
and average daily intake level; 
(d) if so, for how long such guidelines have been followed by 
manufacturers of pesticides; 
(e) whether there is any monitoring committee for supervising 
these pesticides companies; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HU KUMDEO NARAYAN YA DAV): (a) and (b) 
No, Sir. The consumption of chemic al pesticides in the country has 
actually come down from 75,033 MT  (Technical Grade) during 1990-
91 to 47,020 MT during 2001-02. The above reduction in consumption 
of pesticides has been a result of the active interest and initiatives 
taken by the Government to reduce the use of chemical pesticides in 
agriculture in the country and substitution thereof by eco-friendly bio-
pesticides and bio-control agents through the Integrated Pest 
Management which has been adopted by the Government as the main 
plank of plant protection in the country. Apart from promoting the 
Integrated Pest Management, the Government has also been 
periodically reviewing the continued use/ restriction/ban of specific 
pesticides reported to be hazardous by appointing Expert Committees. 
(c) and (d) The Registration Committee (RC) constituted under 
the Insecticides Act, 1968 registers the pesticides after satisfying itself 
about the effectiveness of the prod uct against the target pest and 
safety to human beings, animals and environment. While registering 
pesticides, the Registration Committee approves the usages including 
waiting period between last spray of the pesticides and the harvest. If 
pesticides are used as per recommendations of 
80 

[1 August, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
the Registration Committee and waiting period is. observed, it would 
not leave excessive residues on treated crops. 
Keeping in view the growing concern regarding pesticides 
residues, the Government started an All India Coordinated Research 
Project on Pesticide Residues with 17 Coordinated centres all over 
the country during 1984-85, with a view to develop protocols for safe 
use of pesticides by recommending Good Agricultural Practices, 
based on multi-location supervised field trials. In addition, Maximum 
Residues Limits (MRLs) for various insecticides are also fixed under 
the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. 
Further, the Government is promoting the Integrated Pest 
Management (IPM) strategy in overall crop production programmes. 
Under IPM programme, the use of non-chemical methods including 
bio-pesticides and bio-control agents is being encouraged. The 
manufacturers of pesticides being encouraged. The manufactures of 
pesticides in the country are gover ned by the provisions of the. 
Insecticides Act, 1968 and the Rules framed thereunder. 
(e) and (f) The Directors of Agriculture of respective States issue 
licenses for the manufacture of pesticides in their States after the 
registration is granted by the Registration Committee (RC). They are 
also drawing pesticides samples from the Manufacturing Units as well 
as from Distribution Points for laboratory testing to ensure quality of 
pesticides, besides creating awareness amongst farming community 
regarding -safe and judicious use of pesticides.

Availability of Mackerel colonies 
1353. SHRI YADL APATI VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether huge colonies of mackerel have been located in the 
Bay of Bengal off the Visakhapatnam coast; 
(b) whether investigation has been carried out to identify 
reasons for abundant availability; and 
(c) the action taken to export t he excess catch of mackerel to 
foreign countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI HU KUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. Heavy landings of Indian mackerel by mechanized boats 
operating from Visakhapatnam fishing harbour has been reported 
during the months of January-April, 2003. The investigation showed 
that the concentrations were mainly found in the areas of Pudimadaka 
and Bhimunipatnam at a depth range of 40-50 mts. It has been 
reported that though the mackerel is an important fishery along the 
west coast of India, high incidence of shoals of this fish along the West 
Bengal, Orissa and Andhra Pradesh coast is not uncommon. The 
scientific investigations points to fluctuation in sea surface 
temperature, shortage of food in upper mixed layers and sinking of 
mixed layers during north-east monsoon as probable reasons for 
abundant availability of mackerel in this region. 
(c) Due to the incr eased availability, the export of frozen 
mackerel has recorded almost four-fold increase from the port of 
Visakhapatnam, both in terms of  quantity and value. Besides, a 
substantial quantity is being transported to the metropolitan cities in 
the neighbouring States in fresh/iced form. Curing and drying is also 
practiced for preservation and movement of excess catch to distant 
destinations.

Suicide by students 
1417. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: W ill the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a number of students have committed 
or tried to commit suicide after finding that their results for X and XII 
classes examinations of CBSE this year were below expectations; 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
(c) whether Government would order revaluation of their papers 
to ascertain if there were any human or mechanical errors in the 
valuation of their papers; 
(d) if no, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) steps proposed to be taken to avoid recurrence of such 
incidents? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. VALLABHBHAI RAMJIBHAI 
KATHIRIA): (a) and (b) No, Sir. 
(c) and (d) As per the CBSE's ex amination bye-laws there is no 
provision for revaluation. However, errors in totaling and posting of 
marks are corrected during verification. Unevaluated questions are 
also evaluated during the verification. In order to ensure that there are 
no human or mechanical errors in t he evaluation of papers, the CBSE 
has taken the following important measures: 
(i) Evaluation is done centrally at specified places under the 
close supervision of Head Examiner and Additional Head 
Examiner. Under every Head Examiner only 10-15 
examiners are deputed for evaluation. 
(ii) The evaluators are provid ed with the detailed Marking 
Scheme which is prepared in participation with the 
evaluators, subject experts so that  is no subjectivity or inter-
examiner variability in evaluation. 
(iii) A team of two coordinat ors is appointed at every nodal 
evaluation center to check that no question or part thereof is 
left unevaluated by the examiner s and that the posting and 
totaling of marks is accurate. 
143 

RAJYA  SABHA [1 August, 2003] 
(iv) As an additional precauti onary measure the marks awarded 
to the candidates on the answer scripts are again matched 
with the marks written on the award sheets in the CBSE 
office before supplying the marks to the computer for 
processing of results. 
(v) After the declaration of results, the candidates can apply for 
verification of marks. In verification the answer books of the 
candidates are checked with a view to ensuring that no 
question or part thereof is left unevaluated, posting and 
totaling of marks is accurate. 
(e) CBSE has taken following meas ures to reduce examination 
related stress and anxiety which at times may become the cause of 
suicide among students:- 
• Publication of sample question papers and marking schemes 
to familiarize teachers and students about the nature of 
questions and question papers. 
• Elimination of overall aggregation of marks to reduce 
unhealthy competition among students. 
• Introduction of comprehensive and continuous school based 
evaluation. 
• Providing facility of compar tment examination for Calss X 
and XII. 
• Restructuring of question paper in the important subjects. 
• Providing tele-counseling through helpline close to the 
examination and after the declaration of results.

(i)  A non-lapsable Special Railway Safety Fund (SRSF) of Rs. 
17,000 crores has been set up to wipe out the arrears of 
replacement of over aged assets like track, bridges, rolling 
stock, and signalling ge ars within a fixed time frame of six 
years. The fund has been operational since October 2001. 
(ii)  Extended field trials of pr ototype Anti Collision Device (ACD) 
have been successfully completed on Northern Railway. 
Works for provision of ACD covering about 3500 route kms 
on Northeast Frontier, Souther n, South Central, South 
Western and Northern Railways have been sanctioned. ACD 
survey for 10,000 route kms has also been sanctioned. 
(iii)  Fouling Mark to Fouling Mark track circuiting on entire 'A', 'B', 
'C, 'D' and 'D Spl.' route where speed is more than 75 kmph 
has been completed. 
(iv) Auxiliary Warning System  has been working on Mumbai 
suburban sections. 
(v)  Last vehicle check by Axle  Counter has been introduced on 
over 200 block sections and is being progressively added. 
(vi) To meet the situation arising out of track stresses and 
fatigue, upgradation of track stru cture whenever called for is 
being undertaken on a planned ba sis by utilization of 60-kg 
rails on concrete sleepers. The specifications of rail steel 
have been upgraded and are in conformity with the 
International Union of Railways (UIC) specifications. 
(vii) For improving maintenance and better asset reliability, 
Railways are continuing to eliminate fish-plated joints on 
tracks by welding rails to convert all single rails into long 
welded rails to the extent possible. During relaying/ 
construction of new lines/gauge conversion, long welded

Technique for examining DNA 
1467. SHRI RAMA MUNI RE DDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the 
Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that  scientists of CCMB, Hyderabad, 
have discovered a new technique for examining DNA; 
(b) if so, the details of this new technique; and 
(c) how it would help in catching the poachers of animals? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) and (b) Yes, 
Sir. The technique is based on the indigenously developed novel 
universal primers, to amplify and sequence a specific fragment of 
mitochondrial cytochrome b gene from vast range of animal species in 
a universal manner. The amplified product obtained from a 
confiscated biological sample, is in fact the molecular signature of the 
species of sample in question. The comparison of this signature with 
the signatures of known animal sp ecies available in the database of 
signatures, generated and maintained by CCMB, reveals the identity 
of the unknown sample beyond a reasonable doubt. 
(c) Establishing species identify of confiscated animals is a great 
challenge to law enforcement agencies. The technique developed at 
CCMB is able to establish exact identity of confiscated animals(s) or 
part(s) and product(s) thereof. This DNA-based approach, without any 
prior information about the history of a forensic sample, is able to 
establish whether a drop of blood, tiny piece of meat or bunch of hairs 
belong to human or animal, and if animal, to which species of the 
animal.

1471. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is any mechanism to forecast cyclones in 
advance; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the number of days in advance 
cyclone forecasting is being done presently; 
(c) whether Government have taken any steps to improve the 
accuracy of cyclone forecasts; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) Yes, 
Madam. 
(b) to (d) The India Meteorological Department (IMD) follows a 
four-stage warning system for tropical cyclone. A "Pre-cyclone Watch" 
is issued whenever a depression forms over the Bay of Bengal or 
Arabian Sea. This is followed by a "Cyclone Alert" issued 2-3 days in 
advance. In the third stage, Cyclone Warnings are issued 1-2 days in 
advance which specify the expected place and time of landfall of the 
tropical cyclone. The final stage is known as "Post-landfall Outlook" 
which is issued 12 hours in advance of landfall. 
The accuracy of cyclone forecasts issued by IMD is generally on 
par with the accuracy of such fo recasts issued by the tropical cyclone 
forecast services of other countries. However, with the

SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the 
Seeds Act, 2000, needs certain amendments and modifications in 
view of certain practical difficulties and the challenges thrown up 
218

I suggest that the following points, as emerged from the seminar, 
may be kept in view while introducing the new legislation:— 
(i) To provide for regulating production in addition to sale, import

second offence mentioned under Section 19 of the Seeds 
Act, 1996.

aforesaid modifications suggested and introduce a comprehensive 
legislation on the Seeds Act at the earliest. Thank you, Sir.

Hardships caused due to the withdrawal of North-East 
Industrial Policy, 1997 
SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE (Assam): The 
Government of India has announced a special Industrial Policy, 
namely, the North-East Industrial Policy, 1997 for the North-Eastern 
region of the country. The policy was developed for encouraging 
setting up of industries in the region. Under the policy, excise duty 
relief was granted to the industries set up in the North-East region. 
These included oil refineries also. 
The Central Government has, through Finance Bill, 2003 
withdrawn the aforesaid policy. On the other hand, it has been 
extended to the States of Jammu an d Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, 
Uttaranchal and Kutch region of Gujarat. 
With the withdrawal of the Nort h-East Industrial Policy, 1997 
completely, or, dilution thereof, by its extension to other States, 
industrialisation process initiated in the North-Eastern States has been 
disturbed, due to long distances in volved in markets, raw material 
sources, distance from the ports, insu rgency, etc. in the region. It is a 
widely accepted apprehension that the industrial sector is not 
preferring the region any more. 
The Government of India is requested to give some relief and 
concessions to North-East region to minimise the hardship caused to 
the region as a result of the withdrawal of excise duty relief. Thank 
you, Sir.

DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the Andhra 
Pradesh Government have accorded very high priority for the 
improvement of road network within  the State. The vehicle population 
in Andhra Pradesh has grown from 24,783 in 1956 to over 36,00,000 
as on today. The road length has increased by only seven times, 
whereas the vehicle population has increased 145 times. 
The Andhra Pradesh Government has increased the budget for 
improving the roads from about Rs. 400 crores in 1995-96 to close to 
Rs. 1500 crores each year in the recent past. The State Government 
has started borrowing Rs. 2500 cror es for upgrading and improving 
about 3400 kms. The State had al so borrowed from NABARD to 
progressively upgrade the roads to all-weather category.

of rural roads to the Roads and Buildings Department for improving 
their quality, and has prepared separ ate schemes for improving these 
roads. As the State Government has limited resources, they have 
been urging the Centre to take matching steps to further consolidate 
the gains of investments in developi ng roads made so far, and the

roads would be accommodated in the Tenth Five Year Plan period.
